This post is a snapshot; the page is the living map. The fastest way to find rung 6 is still to hand the premises to someone who does not share our priors.

articles.title: Avoid These 4 Claude Code Context Antipatterns
articles.description: Four ways to quietly pollute your Claude Code context, and how to fix each one with /clear, /rewind, subagents, and a lean CLAUDE.md.
articles.body_html:
The 4 Context Antipatterns

Claude Code is powerful. However, it is easy to accidentally mess up your own session if you're not careful with context. Anthropic’s Claude Code docs list five common failure patterns. I'm going to go over four of them.

Antipattern 1: The Overstuffed Fridge

You want to build a button. You start Claude Code. Halfway through, you ask Claude something random: "Hey, can you explain OAuth?" Claude answers. You go back to building a button. That's cool, but now your context contains both.

Claude's context is like a fridge. It has finite space. When you mix unrelated stuff in, everything gets harder to find. Quality degrades. Claude re-reads all that OAuth stuff every time you ask about the button. It is not giving 100% attention to the button anymore.

Instead, /clear (aliases: /new or /reset) between unrelated tasks. Doing so wipes context and starts you fresh. Your next task gets Claude's full attention.

If your mind wanders like mine, keep a separate Claude session just for those questions.

You can use /btw for a quick side question. The answer never enters your conversation, so your context stays clean.

A fresh context with a focused prompt is better than a cluttered one.

Antipattern 2: The Correction Rabbit Hole

Claude writes code. The result doesn't look right. You correct it: "Make the button smaller." Good, but something is still off. "Make the edges rounder." Again. Again. By the tenth correction, your context is full of attempts. Claude drowns in noise. Each correction doesn't erase the last one. It adds to the pile. "Instead, can you..." adds a new line. Each line is context spent.

Instead, after two failed attempts, /clear and restart with a better prompt. You want Claude to stay sharp. Don't clutter context with corrections. Make every token count.

Don’t do the tenth “no, try this.” Start fresh instead. This time, be precise: “In SubmitButton.tsx, reduce the button height from 48px to 40px, reduce the horizontal padding from 24px to 16px. Shift it 10px left by changing margin-left from 24px to 14px. Make the corners fully rounded with border-radius: 9999px. Keep the font size.” Include what you learned. A clean slate with a better prompt is better than noisy, endless corrections.

Catch mistakes early. Press Esc to stop Claude mid-action. If a turn already went wrong, press Esc Esc (or /rewind) and roll back to before it. A rewind removes the bad attempt instead of piling a correction on top.

Antipattern 3: The Marco Polo Session

You ask Claude: "Investigate why user authentication is slow." Claude reads files. More files. Then more files. Giant log files! Suddenly your context is thousands of lines deep. Claude explores things that probably don't matter.

Claude is like Marco Polo. It likes to explore, and when it does, it explores wide. Claude can read a lot of files faster than a human, but it also fills context with noise faster than I can fill my shopping cart on Black Friday with stuff I don't need. By the time you get an answer, your context is filled up with expedition notes.

Scope the investigation. Or hand it off. Instead of "Investigate why user authentication is slow," say: "Look only at the session lookup in src/auth/. Find slow database queries." Claude now has boundaries and it explores narrow.

Maybe you don't know the boundaries. If you want it to search far and wide, use a subagent. Ask: “Use a subagent to investigate why the login endpoint is slow. Read the relevant files and report back a summary.” The subagent explores in its own context. You get a clean summary. All the file-reading stays in the agent's context, not in your main conversation.

To spawn an investigation in the background while you work on the main task, use /subtask (requires Claude Code v2.1.212 or later). /subtask investigate why user authentication is slow forks a subagent that inherits your current conversation and reports back when it’s done. A subagent is like delegating to an assistant. "Go figure this out. Come back with a summary." The assistant can explore far and wide and that context stays with it. It never enters the main conversation. What comes back is just the brief result.

Antipattern 4: The Overstocked Staples

If Claude's context is your fridge, CLAUDE.md is your staples: milk, eggs, butter (almost every fridge has them, and almost every meal starts from them). Claude loads CLAUDE.md into every session, so whatever you put there takes up space in every conversation.

The problem starts when you have too many “staple” items. Do you really need 2% milk, 1% milk, and whole milk? Maybe just pick one. Do you need four half-empty bottles of different hot sauces instead of one? Do you need a dozen regular-sized eggs and a dozen large cage-free eggs?

Pretty soon you can't find your hot sauce and your milk spoils. A bloated CLAUDE.md works similarly. Important rules get lost in the noise. Claude starts ignoring half of them. Like that milk, old rules go stale. Anthropic suggests keeping each CLAUDE.md under 200 lines. For each line, ask: “Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?” If Claude does fine without it, cut it.

Keep in mind that splitting CLAUDE.md into @imports doesn’t save space. Imported files load at launch too.

Instead, turn knowledge or workflows you only need sometimes into a skill, which Claude loads only when it’s relevant. Rules for one part of the codebase belong in a path-scoped rule, which loads only when Claude touches matching files. A rule that must happen every single time belongs in a hook.

The Pattern

These antipatterns share one theme: context pollution. Claude's context is filled with unrelated tasks, failed corrections, endless exploration, and instructions it doesn't need. Claude's output degrades not because Claude got dumb, but because it’s wading through noise and has less room to think.

Treat these as guardrails. Use them so Claude doesn't get sloppy. Context is your most limited resource. Don't pollute it.

articles.title: I used AI to cheat my way to a 156-day reading streak
articles.description: I asked Codex to recover my Apple Books reading streak. Here is how a C bridge called private Swift APIs to turn two days into 156. Yes, this is cheating.
articles.body_html:
I asked Codex to recover my Apple Books reading streak. Very important engineering work, obviously.

Books showed two days. I had an 80-day run in the history, then a gap, then a few scattered reading days. It happens to the best of us. The app was reporting exactly what it had recorded. I wanted the old streak back anyway, so I asked an agent to fill the gap.

It ended up showing 156 days and New Record. I have read so much.

Before we go any further: don't try this at home. This is cheating. Do actual reading. The agent added reading time to dates that were below the goal. Those entries were manufactured. Nobody read 71 extra days while a script was running.

But the process was interesting. It involved private Swift APIs, backups, a background process, and, of course, a cache. Apparently even my questionable reading decisions need cache invalidation.

Start with the embarrassing part

My daily goal was one minute. One minute. Apple Books was already being very generous with me. Had it on 15 mins a day, but I had to travel and reduced to 1 minute (talk about commitment issues).

The old streak ran from May 11 through July 29, 2026. Continuing it through October 13 would make 156 calendar days. Of those, 85 already met their goals: the original 80, plus five later dates. That left 71 dates to fill.

Seventy had no daily record. August 1 had six seconds, so it needed another 54. How do you even get six seconds of reading? IDK. A date that already met its goal needed no changes, even if it contained much more reading time.

The calculation was small enough:

# Pseudocode
for day in requested_range:
    goal = stored_goal(day, default=60)
    recorded = recorded_seconds(day, default=0)
    additional = max(0, goal - recorded)

    if additional:
        increment_reading_time(day, additional, default_goal=60)

The dates also needed the correct timezone. The edits used America/El_Salvador and local noon, keeping each increment inside its intended calendar day. It would be a pretty annoying way to discover a timezone bug, after going through all this to change a number. A big part of this was possible (within the 5 hour window of my $20 codex subscription) thanks to the work previously done to understand the Apple books data model. Give it a read if you want to read about sqlite databases.

The Apple Books data model
Kevin Alemán
Kevin Alemán
Jun 22

The Apple Books data model

#macos #sqlite #programming #database
1 reaction Comments Add Comment
6 min read

Now, let's start.

Make the backup before getting clever

The history file involved was:

~/Library/Group Containers/group.com.apple.iBooks/CRDTModelLocalFile/ReadingHistoryModel

Before changing it, Codex backed up the history, its context and sync metadata, and the relevant Books preferences. The SQLite context databases were copied through SQLite's backup API. A permanent backup went into Documents, separate from the scratch files.

Then the experiments happened on copies. That was useful because some of the first attempts at calling Apple's private Swift code failed.

An agent having access to your files is a good reason to make the original easy to restore. Keep the backup somewhere separate, give it a name you understand, and be clear about which dates the agent is allowed to change. In this case, the scope was the missing goal time within one specific streak.

The C bridge that called Apple's Swift code

This was the part I wanted to understand properly. Codex found an operation in the installed frameworks:

ReadingHistoryModel.incrementReadingTime(date:amount:defaultGoal:)

But having a method name and calling the method are two separate problems. There was no available SDK module to import for this private interface. The tool used a C bridge to load the framework, resolve the Swift entry points, and call them with the required binary calling convention.

The calls went in both directions. The Swift driver called ordinary C functions declared in native.h. Those C functions called Apple's compiled Swift functions through typed function pointers. The framework was loaded at runtime with dlopen; the C object file was linked into the driver at build time.

Below is the complete C bridge used in this experiment, split into pieces so the explanation can stay next to the code. These are the actual functions and symbols used on this Mac. The Swift snippets are excerpts from the driver.

Start with the C interface

native.h

#include <stdint.h>
typedef struct { uint64_t a, b; } Bits;
void *history_decode(uint64_t a, uint64_t b);
Bits history_describe(void *model);
Bits history_encode(void *model);
void history_increment(void *model, double date, int64_t amount, int64_t goal);
void *history_error(void);
void *history_type(void);
void history_set_streak(void *model, void *dictionary_metadata, void *date, int64_t length);

Bits carries two 64-bit words across the C boundary. On this installation, that matched the representation used for the Data arguments and the Data and String results involved in these calls. Those words can contain storage references or inline information; they are the Swift value's representation, rather than a byte-buffer API.

The C interface exposes opaque pointers for the model and its metadata. The driver uses history_error() to retrieve a captured Swift error and history_type() when reflecting on the model later.

Tell Clang how to call Swift

native.c — attributes, function types, and symbol lookup

#include "native.h"
#include <dlfcn.h>
#include <assert.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#define SWIFT __attribute__((swiftcall))
#define SELF __attribute__((swift_context))
#define ERROR __attribute__((swift_error_result))
#define RESULT __attribute__((swift_indirect_result))
typedef struct { void *value; uintptr_t state; } MetadataResponse;
typedef MetadataResponse (*MetadataFn)(uintptr_t) SWIFT;
typedef void (*DecodeFn)(void * RESULT, uint64_t, uint64_t, void *, void *, void * SELF, void ** ERROR) SWIFT;
typedef Bits (*BitsFn)(void * SELF) SWIFT;
typedef Bits (*EncodeFn)(void *, void *, void *, void *, void * SELF, void ** ERROR) SWIFT;
typedef void (*IncrementFn)(void *, int64_t, int64_t, void * SELF) SWIFT;
static void *metadata, *witness, *last_error;
void *history_error(void) { return last_error; }
void *history_type(void) { return metadata; }
static void *symbol(const char *name) {
    void *value = dlsym(RTLD_DEFAULT, name);
    if (!value) { fprintf(stderr, "Missing symbol: %s\n", name); exit(1); }
    return value;
}

The attributes carry the calling-convention information:

Macro Role in the bridge
SWIFT Call the function using Swift's calling convention
SELF Give the context parameter its special Swift ABI treatment
RESULT Pass storage for an indirectly returned value
ERROR Receive the error result from a throwing Swift call

What's ABI

No, it's not the name of a girl ;) even tho it may be. ABI stands for Application Binary Interface. In short, it defines how already compiled Swift code interacts at the binary level and how the code talks to the runtime.
Type layout conventions, representation, metadata, etc.
You can find way more about this on the web, and probably better explained :)

Clang still needs a function type that describes the lowered arguments correctly. swiftcall handles their low-level placement; the bridge must supply indirect pointers, generic arguments, context, and error parameters in the right shape. The Clang attribute reference documents this distinction.

The symbol() helper resolves an address with dlsym. The $s... strings are Swift's mangled symbol names. They carry information about the module, type, operation, and signature. One of the names used here can be inspected with:

xcrun swift-demangle --compact '$s13BookDataStore19ReadingHistoryModelV09incrementD4Time4date6amount11defaultGoaly10Foundation4DateV_S2itF'

The result identifies ReadingHistoryModel.incrementReadingTime(date:amount:defaultGoal:). Finding that address gives us a place to call. The typedef determines how the call gets there.

Decode a type C doesn't know about

native.c — loading and decoding

void *history_decode(uint64_t a, uint64_t b) {
    assert(dlopen("/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/BookDataStore.framework/BookDataStore", RTLD_NOW | RTLD_GLOBAL));
    MetadataFn meta = symbol("$s13BookDataStore19ReadingHistoryModelVMa");
    metadata = meta(0).value;
    void *(*conforms)(void *, void *) = symbol("swift_conformsToProtocol");
    witness = conforms(metadata, symbol("$s9Coherence4CRDTMp"));
    assert(metadata && witness);
    uintptr_t *vwt = ((uintptr_t **)metadata)[-1];
    size_t size = vwt[8];
    assert(size > 0 && size < 4096);
    void *model = calloc(1, size);
    void *error = NULL;
    DecodeFn decode = symbol("$s9Coherence4CRDTPAAE14serializedDatax10Foundation0D0V_tKcfC");
    decode(model, a, b, metadata, witness, metadata, &error);
    if (error) { last_error = error; return NULL; }
    fprintf(stderr, "Native model decoded (%zu bytes)\n", size);
    return model;
}

dlopen loads BookDataStore. RTLD_GLOBAL makes its loaded exports available to the subsequent RTLD_DEFAULT lookups; the required Coherence symbols were available through the loaded dependencies.

The metadata accessor returns the runtime type information for ReadingHistoryModel. MetadataResponse models its pointer-and-state result; meta(0).value keeps the metadata pointer. swift_conformsToProtocol then retrieves its conformance to Coherence.CRDT. That conformance is represented by a witness table: the information the generic decoder needs to use this particular type's implementation.

C also needs somewhere to put the decoded value. The pointer immediately before the metadata points to its value witness table, which includes layout and value-management information. The bridge reads the size slot used by this ABI, allocates storage, and passes it as the indirect result. The decoded model occupied 24 bytes in this run. Swift's type metadata documentation describes the metadata and value witness table relationship.

The decoder call has more arguments than its Swift source-level spelling suggests. It receives the output storage, the two Data words, generic type metadata, the protocol witness table, the initializer's metatype context, and the error result. The metadata pointer appears twice because those are distinct roles in this entry point.

The driver supplied the Data representation like this:

import Foundation

let arguments = CommandLine.arguments
guard arguments.count >= 3 else { fatalError("input output [increments.json]") }
let data = try Data(contentsOf: URL(fileURLWithPath: arguments[1]))
precondition(MemoryLayout<Data>.size == MemoryLayout<Bits>.size)
let bits = unsafeBitCast(data, to: Bits.self)
guard let model = history_decode(bits.a, bits.b) else {
    let error = unsafeBitCast(history_error()!, to: (any Error).self)
    print("Native decode failed: \(error)")
    exit(1)
}

unsafeBitCast reinterprets the value's bits. The size check catches a size mismatch, but it does not establish that an arbitrary Swift type can safely be passed this way. This bridge depended on the representation and ownership behavior of these specific calls.

Inspect and serialize the model

native.c — description and encoding

Bits history_describe(void *model) {
    BitsFn describe = symbol("$s13BookDataStore19ReadingHistoryModelV16debugDescriptionSSvg");
    return describe(model);
}
Bits history_encode(void *model) {
    EncodeFn encode = symbol("$s9Coherence11CRMergeableP14serializedData_7version10Foundation0D0VAA9CRContextC_AA16CRCodableVersionOtKFTj");
    void *(*conforms)(void *, void *) = symbol("swift_conformsToProtocol");
    void *mergeable_witness = conforms(metadata, symbol("$s9Coherence11CRMergeableMp"));
    assert(mergeable_witness);
    MetadataFn context_meta = symbol("$s9Coherence9CRContextCMa");
    void *(*create_context)(void * SELF) SWIFT = symbol("$s9Coherence9CRContextC6sharedACvgZ");
    void *context = create_context(context_meta(0).value);
    uint8_t version = *(uint32_t *)symbol("$s9Coherence16CRCodableVersionO8version3yA2CmFWC");
    void *error = NULL;
    Bits bits = encode(context, &version, metadata, mergeable_witness, model, &error);
    if (error) { last_error = error; return (Bits){0,0}; }
    return bits;
}

history_describe calls the model's debug-description getter. The Swift driver interprets the returned Bits as a String and uses that description in its round-trip checks.

Encoding uses a separate CRMergeable conformance, its serialization dispatch thunk, and the shared CRContext. The bridge resolves the installed enum case tag for version3 and passes its address to the encoder. That tag lookup and argument representation were checked for this installation.

Both throwing calls start with a null error pointer. On failure, the bridge captures the returned error for the driver. On success, encoding returns the representation of a Swift Data value, which the driver writes to a scratch file and decodes again before any live replacement.

The increment, and the pointer that mattered

native.c — adding reading time

void history_increment(void *model, double date, int64_t amount, int64_t goal) {
    IncrementFn increment = symbol("$s13BookDataStore19ReadingHistoryModelV09incrementD4Time4date6amount11defaultGoaly10Foundation4DateV_S2itF");
    increment(&date, amount, goal, model);
}

This is the function that added the missing seconds. The driver already had the intended day and the amount needed to reach its goal:

history_increment(
    model,
    date.timeIntervalSinceReferenceDate,
    Int64(edit["amount"]!),
    60
)

The important detail in C is increment(&date, amount, goal, model).

For this entry point on the installed build, Swift expected Date indirectly. Its storage contained the reference-date time interval, so the wrapper put that value in a local double and passed its address. The model pointer received the Swift context treatment specified by SELF. The int64_t arguments also assumed the 64-bit Swift.Int representation used on this Mac.

An earlier attempt declared the date as a directly passed double. The scratch process crashed inside Calendar.component(_:from:), attempting to read address 0x3c: decimal 60, one of the other argument values. The callee was reading the wrong thing as its date pointer. A small Swift probe compiled to LLVM IR confirmed the indirect date argument.

That's a fairly concrete reason to inspect the calling convention before trusting a function-pointer cast. The compiler can accept the cast while the call is still wrong.

Update the record dictionary

native.c — adding streak milestones

void history_set_streak(void *model, void *dictionary_metadata, void *date, int64_t length) {
    intptr_t (*offset)(void *, intptr_t) = symbol("swift_reflectionMirror_recursiveChildOffset");
    intptr_t field_offset = offset(metadata, 1);
    assert(field_offset == 8);
    void (*set)(void *, void *, void *, void * SELF) SWIFT = symbol("$s9Coherence15CRDictionary_v1Vyq_Sgxcis");
    set(date, &length, dictionary_metadata, (char *)model + field_offset);
}

The Swift driver reflected on the decoded model, checked that the selected field was named streakRecords, and obtained its dictionary type metadata. On this build, it was CRDictionary_v1<Int, Date>.

The C helper asks for the field's offset, asserts the observed eight-byte offset, and calls the installed dictionary setter. The setter gets the optional date value, the integer key, the dictionary metadata, and the address of the dictionary field as its Swift context.

The date argument here is a pointer to the actual Swift Date? representation. The driver prepared it with:

var date: Date? = start.addingTimeInterval(Double(length-1)*86400)
withUnsafeMutablePointer(to: &date) {
    history_set_streak(model, dictionaryMetadata, $0, Int64(length))
}

That allowed the native setter to add milestones 81 through 156 while keeping the existing records. The field index, offset, dictionary type, and symbol name are all assumptions that need checking on another build.

Build the bridge and the driver

In the scratch directory, the build commands were:

clang -c native.c -o native.o

swiftc \
  -module-cache-path /private/tmp/books-streak-recovery/module-cache \
  -import-objc-header native.h \
  repair.swift native.o -o repair

-import-objc-header exposes the C declarations to the Swift driver; the header itself contains ordinary C. Linking native.o supplies those helper implementations. The private Swift entry points are resolved later, when the running tool loads the framework.

The full driver also handled the requested dates, error reporting, serialization, and verification. The snippets above focus on the language boundary.

Keep the assumptions visible

This was a short-lived repair process with global state and build-specific layout assumptions. It leaves decoded allocations alive until process exit. A reusable library would need proper Swift value destruction, ownership and alignment handling, allocation checks, and a fuller error lifecycle. But the goal is to not make this an habit and start reading like a functional human being

There is also a very practical footgun in the actual code: dlopen sits inside assert. These builds had assertions enabled. Defining NDEBUG would remove the framework load along with the check; a maintained implementation should load it separately and handle failure explicitly.

The code is here because it explains what made the experiment work. It should also explain why I keep saying to leave your reading-history files alone.

And then Books still said two days

After the daily entries were filled, Books recognized another completed day in the current week. The streak still said two days. The record still said 80.

Of course there was more state. It's Apple, there should be something else, somewhere.

Three pieces needed to agree:

  • The daily history needed enough credited time for the missing dates.
  • streakRecords needed the newly reached streak lengths and their dates.
  • ReadingHistory.CurrentStreak needed the new cached count.

The record dictionary ended at 80 days. Codex preserved those entries and added milestones 81 through 156, dated July 30 through October 13. We had to populate this data too.

Swift reflection identified the record field and its dictionary type, and the bridge used the installed dictionary implementation's setter. Another check confirmed that these changes left the daily history unchanged. Finally, with Books closed, the cached count was updated:

BOOKS_PREFS="$HOME/Library/Containers/com.apple.iBooksX/Data/Library/Preferences/com.apple.iBooksX.plist"

defaults write "$BOOKS_PREFS" ReadingHistory.CurrentStreak -int 156

That command only handles the cache. The daily records and streak milestones had already been edited. ReadingHistory.LastStreakDate already contained 20261013, so it stayed unchanged.

Make the app use the edited history

Books and bookdatastored can keep history in memory. Editing the file while they're using it creates an opportunity for a later write to replace your changes. Then we had to close Books app for the cache to be read again.

Before replacement, the live daily history was compared with the version used to prepare the edits. The validated file was staged beside the live one, given the same permissions, flushed, and installed with os.replace. The cache was refreshed while Books remained closed.

Opening Books started the helper again. This time, Reading Goals showed 156 days, a 156-day record, and New Record.

The checks covered both the file and the app. The serialized output was decoded again, its model description was compared with the in-memory result, and every daily date, time, and goal was checked. The app then confirmed that it was displaying the intended result. FINALLY!

The advice I should probably follow

There's an awkward connection to my last article about AI. I wrote about how much easier it is becoming to produce a result, and how we still need to pay attention to the work and understanding behind it:

The future, after AI
Kevin Alemán
Kevin Alemán
Oct 8

The future, after AI

#ai #programming #career #beginners
2 reactions Comments 1 comment
6 min read

Here I was, asking an agent to produce a very impressive number in a book app. It did the software work. It inspected the state, made the edits, and checked the result. My reading habit still needs me to open a book tomorrow, but I'll start from 156 rather than 2 ;)

If you want something practical to do with Books, set a daily goal you can actually meet. On the Mac, that's under Home → Reading Goals → Adjust Goal. Then read. After a missed day, start another streak.

Gotta be honest: my reading goal was 1 minute and even with that low value, I couldn't do it (commitment issues? who?).

The fun lesson, as always, is: you can have the streak you want. It's just a number. The actual value is never in the milestone, is what you learn in the road :)

articles.title: There's No AI Agent, Nor Any Harness.
articles.description: There's no AI agent, nor any harness. There's just software using machine learning models.
articles.body_html:
Don't let them make you forget about software.

There's no AI agent, nor any harness. These are just buzz words coined to take the emphasis away from software and software development.

There's just software, machine learning models made using software, and software that makes good use of those models.

If you divide the digital world into:

  1. Software: deterministic programming + non-tensor data e.g. control logic, user inputs, databases, APIs, heuristics etc.

  2. Machine Learning Models

Then, every digital AI system that exists today completely falls in either of those two categories, often both.

There is no mystical third element!

Everything running on servers (CPU / GPU) consists entirely of traditional software, and tensor-based models. Nothing more.

The funny part is: most users never get even close to those models. All they use are software that use those models, and then call it Agent, Harness, etc. etc.

Models don't even do any tool calls either! They only accept input (text, image, audio, video) and return output (text, image, audio, video).

That's all there is to it. It's the software that makes the tool calls based on what the models return.

The models don't have any control over what happens after it returns something.

We do it using the software we developed, software uses those models, then the users do it based on those software.

Once you understand this, use those buzz words when you need to, but every once in a while, remind people of what they are actually using under the hood.

P.S. of course, most developers are already aware of the under the hood architecture of the whole thing. However, what most people are probably not aware of, is the fact that, even switching the word software with terms like "agent" and "harness" devalues our work to people who don't know any better. That's why, saying out loud what it is, at least some of the times, is important. 🥰

Fayaz

A Software Engineer who strongly believes you can add immense value by knowingly implementing Software Engineering best practices even at the age of AI, and puts human life and dignity above all else.

articles.title: Your AI review bot is training you to ignore it
articles.description: AI code review backfires through noise. A bot that fires on style nits and speculation trains reviewers to scroll past it — exactly when it finds something real.
articles.body_html:
A year ago we turned on an AI reviewer for every PR. Last month we turned most of it off. Not because it was wrong — because it was noisy, and noise is how a review tool loses its teeth.

The decay is predictable

Week one: everyone reads every comment. Week three: the bot flags a formatting nit on line 41, a possible null on line 88, and a question about a variable name. Two of three are bikesheds. By week six, you scroll to the bottom to see if it blocked the merge, and skip the rest.

That's the trap. The bot isn't lying to you. It's just running every check it knows on every diff, and most of those checks have low precision. So the signal-to-noise ratio decays until the comments become wallpaper.

Then it catches a real one — and nobody reads it.

Precision beats recall here

For a review bot, recall is the wrong target. You don't want it to find everything; you want the things it does say to be worth stopping for. A bot that is right 80% of the time it speaks gets read. A bot that is right 40% of the time it speaks gets trained into the background.

The lever is turning down low-confidence rules. Style nits belong in the linter, not a PR comment. Speculation about intent belongs in a suggestion, not a blocking thread. The bot should be quiet by default and loud only when it has something mechanical and high-confidence.

Where the high-confidence stuff lives

The checks that survive the cull are the ones with ground truth. Not "this might be unsafe," but "the code returns 200 but the contract says 201" — a fact, checkable against a machine-readable source. Those have near-zero false positives, so when the bot speaks, it always means it.

For API changes that check is contract drift, and it's the kind of thing that's cheap to run locally and impossible for a human to eyeball. We kept that one. The variable-name comments went.

What to do this week

Open your review bot's history and count, per rule, how often a human pushed back or ignored it. The rules with the lowest strike rate get turned off first. You'll end up with a bot that comments on one in five PRs instead of every PR — and when it does, people read it.

A reviewer that nobody reads is worse than no reviewer, because it creates the feeling of coverage. How long has it been since you actually read every comment your AI reviewer left?

articles.title: Building Quidra: A Programming Language Designed for Maximum Meaning Per Token
articles.description: What if shorter code isn't always better?   I'm building Quidra, an experimental,...
articles.body_html:
What if shorter code isn't always better?

I'm building Quidra, an experimental, open-source programming language guided by one idea: Maximum Meaning Per Token (MMPT).

The goal isn't to make every program as short as possible. It's to remove unnecessary ceremony while keeping the information that helps humans, compilers, and code-generating tools understand what a program actually does.

Quidra is statically typed, implemented in C++20, and uses LLVM for native compilation. It isn't a Python wrapper or a transpiler to another high-level language.

Try it: Playground · GitHub · Website

Less syntax, but not less meaning

Consider mutation. A short function call can hide an important fact: the function might change the variable you pass to it.

In Quidra, mutable access to existing storage is explicit at both ends:

void increment(int &value)
    value += 1

int count = 7
increment(&count)

print(count)
print(NL)

The parameter int &value declares writable access. The call increment(&count) makes that authority visible to the reader without requiring them to inspect the implementation.

Yes, & is an extra token. But it conveys a distinction that can affect correctness. To me, that's a good trade.

Assignment should not secretly create aliases

Quidra uses value semantics for ordinary assignments:

int[] original = [1, 2, 3]
int[] copy = original

copy[0] = 9

Changing copy doesn't change original.

The compiler and runtime are free to optimize the implementation, including with copy-on-write, as long as observable behavior stays the same. The point is not to force expensive physical copies; it's to give assignment a predictable meaning.

Tensor shapes belong in contracts

In numerical computing, many errors come from assumptions about tensor shapes that never appear in function signatures.

Quidra can express shape constraints directly in a type:

real32 first_sample(const tensor<real32>{3, _, _} pixels)
    return pixels[0, 0, 0].item()

Here, tensor<real32>{3, _, _} means a tensor with real32 elements, exactly three dimensions, and a first dimension of size 3. The other two dimensions are unconstrained.

The const parameter also communicates that the function doesn't have permission to modify its argument.

Shape information doesn't eliminate every runtime check. But when the compiler can prove a mismatch, I'd rather find out before running the program.

Conversions should be decisions, not surprises

Quidra distinguishes mathematical numeric types from fixed-width representations. For instance, int is arbitrary-precision, while int64 and real64 have specific machine representations.

Converting an existing typed value is explicit:

int value = 10
real64 converted = real64(value)

This can be more verbose than implicit promotion. That's intentional: changing a value's representation may change its range or precision, and the source code should make that decision visible.

Quidra also supports T | error for typed failure and try for propagation, while allowing a fail-fast path when a caller doesn't need to retain the error explicitly. The aim is to make important failure contracts available without surrounding every ordinary operation with ceremony.

A native compiler, not just a syntax experiment

The Quidra compiler is written in C++20 and uses LLVM for native code generation. The project includes a REPL, JIT/AOT execution paths, diagnostics, language tooling, tensors, and automatic differentiation infrastructure.

There are also separate first-party repositories for Math, NN, Vision, Video, and DNN. Quidra is intended to be a general-purpose language, with numerical computing and machine learning as important applications—not its only use cases.

You can find the implementation, specifications, and examples in the GitHub organization.

Can language design make LLM-generated code more reliable?

This is one of the questions motivating Quidra.

LLMs can already write code in established languages. But syntax that is easy to produce isn't necessarily code that is easy to verify or safely modify.

My hypothesis is that explicit mutation, predictable value semantics, checked numeric conversions, and visible shape and error contracts could help both developers and code-generation tools reason about programs.

That is a hypothesis, not a proven advantage. Meaningful comparisons will require controlled experiments and careful attention to how much existing language knowledge an LLM has already learned.

I'm as interested in finding where this approach fails as in finding where it works.

What Quidra isn't (yet)

Quidra is experimental and pre-1.0. Its ecosystem, tooling, and real-world adoption are far smaller than those of Python, Rust, or C++. Some design decisions may change as the implementation and tests evolve.

And explicitness has a cost: sometimes a program needs more characters. MMPT is about meaningful tokens, not winning a character-count contest.

I'd love your feedback—and contributors are welcome

I'm particularly interested in these questions:

  1. Which distinctions deserve explicit syntax, and which can safely be inferred?
  2. Where would these design choices create friction in real programs?
  3. How should we measure whether a language helps people or LLMs write more reliable code?

Quidra is MIT-licensed, and I'm looking for open-source collaborators interested in compilers, C++/LLVM, language design, developer tooling, testing, documentation, math, and ML. You don't have to be a compiler expert: there are approachable first contributions, too.

  • Try Quidra in the Playground
  • Explore the source on GitHub
  • Read the contribution guide
  • Join the contributor discussion

Constructive criticism is very welcome. A language gets better when people try to break its assumptions.

articles.body_html:
Mutative lets you write immutable updates as ordinary mutations. A recipe changes a draft of the state, and Mutative returns the next state, copying only what the recipe changed and sharing the rest with the previous state.

Mutative 2.0 keeps the API of 1.x and changes the work behind it. Picture a worker that takes the first job off a queue of 10,000 jobs and puts it back at the end when it fails. In 1.x, that shift() call moved each of the 9,999 remaining jobs through the draft's proxy. In 2.0, it moves them natively on the draft's copy: with auto-freeze and patches off, removing the first of 10,000 jobs took 7 µs, against 8.2 ms with 1.3.0, more than 1,000 times as long.

Most workloads gain far less. Across the 97 scenarios of the benchmark, 2.0 was 3.6 times as fast as Immer 11.1.18 with matched settings and 4.3 times as fast as 1.3.0, on geometric mean, and slower than Immer in 6 of 614 measured cases.

The changes fall into three areas:

  • Less work on arrays, collections and snapshots. Array methods that move elements run natively, and Set and Map drafts, current() and apply() do less work per update.
  • Correct results in edge cases. Patches follow Immer's order and replay where some 1.x patches failed, Set drafts keep every change, and apply() is stricter about the paths it accepts.
  • Predictable builds and types. Bundlers and Node.js both select the development or production build from process.env.NODE_ENV, and more types match what the code returns.

No function or option was renamed or removed, and no new option is required. This is a major release because observable behavior changes: patch order and values, freezing of Map and Set instances, build selection, production errors and some inferred types. Builds now target ES2018, and several bug fixes change results that 1.x computed incorrectly.


Upgrading from 1.x? The checklist at the end lists what to check, the migration guide describes every change since 1.3.0, and the release notes list the pull requests and contributors of 2.0.

How Mutative works

If Mutative is new to you, this example shows the model. The recipe marks the first job as done. With enablePatches, create() also returns patches that describe the change and inverse patches that undo it, which apply() can replay:

import { apply, create } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  settings: { maxAttempts: 3 },
  queue: [
    { id: 1, done: false },
    { id: 2, done: false },
  ],
};

const [nextState, patches, inversePatches] = create(
  baseState,
  (draft) => {
    draft.queue[0].done = true;
  },
  { enablePatches: true }
);

// The base state is unchanged, and what the recipe did not change is shared.
expect(baseState.queue[0].done).toBe(false);
expect(nextState.queue[0].done).toBe(true);
expect(nextState.settings).toBe(baseState.settings);
expect(nextState.queue[1]).toBe(baseState.queue[1]);

// Patches describe the change, and inverse patches undo it.
expect(patches).toEqual([
  { op: 'replace', path: ['queue', 0, 'done'], value: true },
]);
expect(apply(baseState, patches)).toEqual(nextState);
expect(apply(nextState, inversePatches)).toEqual(baseState);

A draft is a Proxy. The next state holds a shallow copy of each object that the recipe changed and of the objects that lead to it, made at most once per update, and shares every other object with the base state. Reference checks, such as React's memoization or a store's selectors, can then skip what did not change.

Drafts are revoked when the recipe ends, so keep the next state or a current() snapshot, not a draft. The next state is frozen only with enableAutoFreeze: true. Concepts explains the model, and Pitfalls collects its rules.

Less work on arrays, collections and snapshots

Array methods that move elements

In 1.x, array methods ran through the draft's proxy, so shift() read and wrote every remaining element through it. In 2.0, shift(), unshift(), splice() and reverse() move the elements of a plain array directly on the draft's copy. indexOf(), lastIndexOf() and includes() search the current array natively, and sort() and join() run natively on arrays of primitives.

An object of the base state that these methods remove comes back as a draft, so changing it leaves the base state alone. An element that only moves keeps its identity, and the patches replay in both directions. Here is the retry from the introduction, on a short queue:

import { apply, create, isDraft } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  queue: Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, id) => ({ id, attempts: 0 })),
};

const [nextState, patches, inversePatches] = create(
  baseState,
  (draft) => {
    // shift() moves the other jobs natively on the draft's copy and returns
    // the removed job as a draft.
    const job = draft.queue.shift()!;
    expect(isDraft(job)).toBe(true);
    job.attempts += 1;
    draft.queue.push(job);
  },
  { enablePatches: true }
);

expect(nextState.queue.map((job) => job.id)).toEqual([1, 2, 3, 4, 0]);
expect(nextState.queue[4].attempts).toBe(1);
// The base state is unchanged, and the jobs that only moved are shared.
expect(baseState.queue[0].attempts).toBe(0);
expect(nextState.queue[0]).toBe(baseState.queue[1]);
// The patches replay in both directions.
expect(apply(baseState, patches)).toEqual(nextState);
expect(apply(nextState, inversePatches)).toEqual(baseState);

These native paths are built for dense arrays of plain data. Sparse arrays, array subclasses, arrays under a custom mark and methods with callbacks take the proxy path, as do calls in strict mode on arrays that may hold objects, unless they run inside unsafe(). The native methods read getters on array indices as plain values, so a getter may run a different number of times than through the proxy. The FAQ and the [native array method contract][contract] give the details.

Search a snapshot, change the draft

Methods with callbacks, such as find() and filter(), still run through the draft, so a read-only scan may create a draft for every row it visits. For a read-only search of a large array, search a current() snapshot of plain values instead, and change the match through the draft. In 2.0, current() copies a changed array from its current elements rather than reading each one through the draft, and the snapshot keeps the draft's indices after elements move:

import { create, current } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  queue: Array.from({ length: 10_000 }, (_, id) => ({ id, paused: false })),
};

const nextState = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  draft.queue.shift();
  // Search a snapshot of plain values, which creates no drafts, and change
  // the match through the draft.
  const index = current(draft.queue).findIndex((job) => job.id === 9_999);
  draft.queue[index].paused = true;
});

expect(nextState.queue).toHaveLength(9_999);
expect(nextState.queue[9_998]).toEqual({ id: 9_999, paused: true });
expect(nextState.queue[0]).toBe(baseState.queue[1]);

With auto-freeze and patches off, the recipe above took 257 µs, against 15,717 µs with 1.3.0 and 11,255 µs with Immer. When the recipe updates the first row instead of removing it, it took 176 µs with the snapshot search and 2,169 µs with a search through the draft.

Sets, Maps and applying patches

Set and Map updates also do less work. As soon as a recipe read a Set, 1.3.0 mapped every item, and it copied the Set when a lookup missed. 2.0 does neither: like Immer, it answers lookups such as has() and size from the original Set until the recipe changes it. Even then, it edits the Set's copy directly and tracks only the items that have drafts, instead of copying every item into a Map and back. A Map draft's forEach() reads entries from the draft's state rather than through the proxy.

apply() gains from the native array methods too, since it inserts and removes array elements with splice() on a draft. It also reads the type of each draft on a patch path once per step, where it used to ask the proxy twice.

What the benchmark shows

Unless noted, the numbers in this post come from one benchmark batch, run on October 12, 2026, that compared Mutative 2.0 with Mutative 1.3.0 and Immer 11.1.18 in 97 scenarios, with auto-freeze and patches each off and on. A cell is one scenario at one size in one mode; How the numbers were measured gives the rest of the setup.

With matched settings, 2.0 was faster than Immer in 595 of 614 cells, within 5% in 13 and slower in 6, with a geometric mean speedup of 3.58. Against 1.3.0, it was faster in 535 cells, within 5% in 70 and slower in 9, with a geometric mean of 4.27. With each library's defaults, where Immer freezes the next state, Mutative does not, and neither generates patches, 2.0 was faster than Immer in 154 of 157 cells, with a geometric mean of 6.63. These means weight every cell equally, so they describe this suite, not the speed of your application.

The table shows where the gains come from and where they stop. Times are microseconds per scenario, with auto-freeze and patches off unless the row says otherwise; lower is better.

Workload Mutative 2.0 Mutative 1.3.0 Immer 11.1.18
Remove the first of 10,000 rows with shift() 7.04 8,203 7,408
Look up two numbers in a Set of 10,000 and read its size 0.62 544 0.66
Update one object in a Set of 10,000 531 1,024 6,024
Push a row onto 10,000 rows and insert a property, with patches 63.2 210 360
Insert, remove and replace a row of 100 with apply() 2.97 115 99.0
200 RTK Query-style updates 1,001 1,849 1,133
Update one of 10,000 records 1,200 1,188 2,094
Update a field of a class instance with 1,000 fields, with auto-freeze 402 411 237

The RTK Query-style row simulates a reducer for 100 pending and 100 resolved requests, without running Redux Toolkit; in that mix of small updates, 2.0 took about half as long as 1.3.0 and 12% less time than Immer. Updates that spend their time copying one large object, record or Map, like the records row, take about as long as before. And patches add little when an update changes only a few paths: the push-and-insert update took about 63 µs with or without patches, while 1.3.0 went from 65.8 µs to 210 µs and Immer from 161 µs to 360 µs.

Where 2.0 is slower

Against Immer with matched settings, 2.0 was slower in 6 cells, all with auto-freeze. Four update one field of a class instance with many fields: with 1,000 fields, 2.0 took 1.7 times as long, and with 100 or 10,000 fields and without patches, about 5% longer. The [summary][limits] attributes the gap to freezing the copy, which 2.0 builds property by property from descriptors where Immer 11 uses Object.assign(). Without auto-freeze, the update of 1,000 fields took 2.0 either about 98 µs or about 200 µs, depending on the process, against 203 µs for Immer. In the other two cells, which push a row onto 100 rows and prepend rows with concat(), the difference was smaller than the variation between the runs of each library. With each library's defaults, all 3 slower cells return a new state of rows frozen earlier, a case that Auto-freeze and returned values explains.

Against 1.3.0, 2.0 was 8–18% slower in 9 cells, all with auto-freeze, and in all but one of them the difference was smaller than the variation between runs. A hand-written reducer is still faster in most cases: in the 150 cells where the suite's spread-based reference reducer ran, 2.0 was slower in 129 and took 8.4 times as long on geometric mean.

Two other costs are worth knowing. With patches, a Set that adds or deletes items compares all of its items to emit its patches. With auto-freeze off, adding a number to a Set of 10,000 numbers took 440 µs with patches and 29.5 µs without. Browser engines also differ from Node.js: in WebKit 26.4, Object.freeze() of a 10,000-element array took about 2.4 ms and every scan of a frozen array was slow, so an update of 10,000 frozen rows took several milliseconds with every Mutative build measured there. [Tradeoffs and limits][limits] lists the rest, including memory.

Bundle size

Some of this speed is paid for in bytes. Patches, Map and Set support and the native array methods are built into create() rather than offered as plugins, so a bundler cannot drop them. Bundled for the browser in production mode, minified and compressed with Brotli, create() alone takes 7.9 kB, 2.1 kB more than with 1.3.0, against 3.6 kB for produce() from Immer 11.1.21, the latest release when the sizes were measured. create(), apply(), current() and original() together take 8.5 kB, 2.2 kB more than with 1.3.0, against 6.4 kB for their Immer counterparts with its patch, Map/Set and array-method plugins enabled. The [README][readme-performance] records the setup; 1.3.0 was measured the same way.

How the numbers were measured

The batch measured main at commit [40f3a42][measured-commit], before its version changed from 1.3.0 to 2.0.0. The published 2.0.0 package contains the same production file, with the SHA-256 that the summary [records for the measured build][identity], cb6464f3…. The 97 scenarios, which the [benchmark guide][workloads] describes, ran at 100 rows, and 30 of them also at 1,000 and 10,000 rows, on an Apple M1 Max with Node.js 24.16.0, against Mutative 1.3.0 and Immer 11.1.18 from npm. Each library ran each scenario in three processes of its own, and each time is the median of the three process means. With auto-freeze on, the inputs were frozen in advance, so the first freeze of outside data is not timed, and patch measurements use arrayLengthAssignment: false in Mutative to match Immer's index-removal patches.

Immer's opt-in enableArrayMethods() plugin was off. In 11.1.18, as the [audit][audit] shows, and still in 11.1.21, it returns objects of the base state from shift(), pop() and splice(), so editing a removed object, as the retry recipe above does, changes the previous state, and its forward patches can fail to replay. Measured separately with the plugin, Immer was faster in 59 of 328 cells, mostly where it hands base objects to callbacks, which 2.0 never does, and slower in every cell that moves elements.

The [performance summary][summary] records the results, method and limits of the batch. The Performance page and the [latest summary][latest-summary] show current results, and pnpm benchmark:immer runs the suite in a clone of the repository.

Correct results in edge cases

Alongside the speed work, 2.0 fixes cases in which 1.x produced a wrong state or patches that did not replay. These are the fixes most likely to matter; the migration guide lists them all.

Patches

If you record patches for undo, redo or synchronization, expect these differences:

  • Order. Patches of a nested draft come before those of its parents, as in Immer. Applying them gives the same state as before, and the replace patches that only restated an unchanged draft at its original index are gone.
  • Values. A patch value that was a draft is now the object that the next state holds, not a deep copy, so auto-freeze freezes it too. Copy a patch value before you change it.
  • Replay. Patches now replay correctly where those of 1.x could fail or produce a wrong state: after sort() or an assignment moved or replaced a changed draft, when a Set added or removed items and also changed one, when a recipe assigned a draft's original object to the key that holds the draft, and when an array changed between 0 and -0 or shrank and grew again. The migration guide describes each case.

Some fixes change the next state itself. With patches on, when two or more items of a Set below the root changed below their first level, as worker.stats.jobs does here, 1.3.0 kept the change of only one of them. 2.0 keeps every change, and the patches replay in both directions:

import { apply, create } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  workers: new Set([
    { name: 'build-1', stats: { jobs: 1 } },
    { name: 'build-2', stats: { jobs: 2 } },
  ]),
};

const [nextState, patches, inversePatches] = create(
  baseState,
  (draft) => {
    for (const worker of draft.workers) {
      worker.stats.jobs += 1;
    }
  },
  { enablePatches: true }
);

expect([...nextState.workers].map((worker) => worker.stats.jobs)).toEqual([
  2, 3,
]);
expect([...baseState.workers].map((worker) => worker.stats.jobs)).toEqual([
  1, 2,
]);
expect(apply(baseState, patches)).toEqual(nextState);
expect(apply(nextState, inversePatches)).toEqual(baseState);

Some limits remain. When patches add objects to a Set, apply() copies them, so inverse patches cannot remove the copies by their original identity, and added items go to the end, which can shift the positions that later patches address. For repeated undo and redo or synchronization of such collections, use a Map keyed by an id, or an array; see Sets of objects. Applying the patches of a sparse array can also turn its holes into explicit undefined entries.

Applying patches

apply() is also stricter. It now rejects a path that ends in __proto__, as it already rejected __proto__ earlier in a path, and reads a Set item only by its index, so a path can no longer reach Array.prototype through a Set. If you apply patches from sources that you do not control, such as other clients, these checks are a reason to upgrade. Map keys in a path are used as they are, without conversion to strings. Copies of patch values keep their own symbol keys, and an own __proto__ key, such as one from JSON.parse(), stays a plain property. With mutable: true, a patch that replaces the root state now throws, since the state cannot be replaced in place. Patches that apply() accepts lists the rules.

Collections, iterators and failed producers

Set and Map drafts now behave more like the built-ins they stand for. A draft of a Set subclass changes an instance of the subclass, so the subclass's own add(), has(), delete() and clear() take effect during the recipe; its add() must store the value it receives. A Set draft that the recipe moves elsewhere, such as to another key, keeps its changes there. And the iterators of Map and Set drafts work like built-in ones: a partly consumed iterator continues where it stopped, and iterator helpers such as toArray() are available where the engine has them.

These iterators now also end with their draft. A draft lives until its synchronous recipe finishes, until the Promise of its async recipe settles, or until a manual draft's finalize() succeeds. After that, Map value and entry iterators and all Set iterators throw a TypeError instead of yielding another value. Exhausted iterators stay exhausted, and Map.keys() keeps its native iterator, because Map keys are not drafted. Consume these iterators while their draft is active.

A producer that fails after its recipe returned, for example because the recipe changed the draft and also returned another value, now revokes its drafts as a throwing recipe does, and keeps the original error. Manual drafts differ: if finalize() throws, the draft can stay writable, so start a new draft from the base state instead of reusing it; see manual drafts.

Auto-freeze and returned values

With enableAutoFreeze: true, 2.0 freezes Map and Set instances themselves, as Immer does; 1.x only replaced their mutating methods. Later producers skip a frozen collection instead of walking it again, but adding a property to a frozen Map or Set, or replacing one of its methods, now fails.

A recipe can also return a new state. That value may hold drafts, as { ...draft, count: 0 } does, so Mutative searches it for them. With auto-freeze, the production build of 2.0 skips frozen objects in the returned value and everything below them, which makes returning an earlier, frozen state cheap. Development builds still search there and throw when they find a draft, so never put a draft inside a frozen object, or inside anything that a frozen object holds. rawReturn(), which 1.x already had, skips the search for a value that holds no drafts; never wrap one that does.

This search explains the 3 cells in which 2.0 at its defaults was slower than Immer at its defaults. Each returns a new state of rows that were frozen earlier. Immer, which freezes by default, skips those rows, while 2.0 without auto-freeze searches all of them, taking 2.60 ms at 10,000 rows where Immer took 0.79 µs. rawReturn() avoids the search, and with auto-freeze, the production build of 2.0 skips the frozen rows, taking 0.53 µs. Fresh data reverses the result: in a [separate run][fresh] on October 13, 2026, with the same production build, returning 10,000 rows that each call creates took 9.2 ms with Immer's default auto-freeze, 3.1 ms with 2.0 at its defaults, and 0.23 ms with rawReturn().

Predictable builds and types

The package contains a development build, with full error messages, warnings and extra checks, and a minified production build. In 2.0, process.env.NODE_ENV selects between them in bundlers and Node.js:

  • Bundlers resolve the ESM build, whose development checks now test process.env.NODE_ENV. When your production build replaces it with 'production', the bundler drops the development code; in 1.x, the ESM build always ran it.
  • Bundles for Node.js, such as esbuild's with platform: 'node', use the CommonJS entry, which selects a build when it loads. If such a bundle does not define process.env.NODE_ENV, it includes both builds, which more than doubles a minified bundle of create(). Define the variable, or keep Mutative external.
  • Node.js resolves import to a module that re-exports the CommonJS build, so import and require share one instance, which reads NODE_ENV once when it loads. In 1.x, import always ran the development ESM build, as a separate instance.

Browsers, and other environments without a process global, fail with process is not defined when they load dist/mutative.esm.mjs directly. Load dist/mutative.esm.production.min.mjs or the UMD build there instead; see Installation.

Production builds throw Minified Mutative error #<code> with a link to the errors page, which decodes the code. CommonJS consumers already got these errors in 1.x; in 2.0, production bundles get them too, and the errors of apply(), original() and rawReturn() are now coded as well. [BUILDING.md][building] describes the build pipeline.

More checks in development

Production builds skip the development checks, so run your tests with the development build. In 2.0, it also catches these mistakes:

  • Drafts as Map keys. draft.map.set(draft.key, value) throws, since the next state would keep a revoked draft as the key. Use original(draft), current(draft) or an id instead.
  • Keys that string paths cannot name. With enablePatches: { pathAsArray: false }, a patch path that would hold a non-string Map key or a symbol key throws. Keep the default array paths for such keys.
  • Searches through large drafts. In strict mode, a recipe that leaves 1,000 or more drafts unchanged warns once. A current() snapshot can usually replace the search that caused it.

With auto-freeze, the check for circular references now reports only an object that holds itself, so a changed draft that holds its original, as draft.prev = original(draft) makes it, no longer throws. Cycles are still not supported. The errors page lists the messages.

Output and package entries

Every build now targets ES2018 instead of ES2015, which keeps object spread native. Mutative still needs Proxy, and engines that have Proxy but not ES2018 syntax, such as Chrome 49–59, Firefox 18–54, Safari 10–11.0 and Edge 12–18, need Mutative transpiled by your build. The package still declares Node.js 14.0 as its minimum, and CI runs a short test of the packed package on Node.js 14.0.0.

The exports map now gives import and require their own type declarations, so NodeNext resolution gets declarations of the module kind it imports. The [package checks][package-checks] exercise the CommonJS, ESM and UMD builds and both NodeNext and Bundler type resolution. The declarations support TypeScript 5.0 and later.

Types

Several types now match what the code returns. With an explicit state type, an async recipe gives Promise<State>, and so do curried producers of async recipes; 1.x typed the result as State. And apply() accepts enableAutoFreeze: true and returns Immutable<State>, where the types of 1.x rejected the option:

import { apply, create, type Immutable, type Patches } from 'mutative';

type State = { count: number; tags: string[] };

const baseState: State = { count: 0, tags: [] };

// 1.x typed this result as State; 2.0 types it as the Promise that it is.
const pending: Promise<State> = create<State>(baseState, async (draft) => {
  draft.count = await Promise.resolve(1);
});
expect((await pending).count).toBe(1);

// The types of 1.x rejected enableAutoFreeze here; 2.0 types the frozen result.
const patches: Patches = [{ op: 'add', path: ['tags', 0], value: 'v2' }];
const frozen: Immutable<State> = apply(baseState, patches, {
  enableAutoFreeze: true,
});
expect(frozen.tags).toEqual(['v2']);
expect(Object.isFrozen(frozen.tags)).toBe(true);

Curried producers that annotate their draft and return a new state, and recipes that may or may not return a Promise, are also typed more precisely. Generic code has caveats, such as a state type that is itself a type parameter; see TypeScript in the migration guide.

Upgrading from 1.x

The fixes in 2.0 are not backported to 1.x, and 1.3.0 is the last 1.x release. Install 2.0:

npm install mutative@2

Libraries built on Mutative that declare mutative 1.x as a peer dependency make npm 7 and later stop with ERESOLVE when it installs mutative@2 beside them. Install versions of them that accept 2.0, or stay on 1.3.0 until they do.

Then work through these steps. The migration guide lists the changes behind each one.

  1. Run your tests with both builds: the development build, which reports the new checks, and the production build, with NODE_ENV=production. In production, match errors by their codes, not their messages. See Development builds.
  2. Check your bundles and targets. Define process.env.NODE_ENV in every bundle, including bundles for Node.js, or keep Mutative external. Load the production ESM or UMD build in browsers without a bundler, and transpile Mutative for engines without ES2018 syntax. See Build output and package entries.
  3. Update code and tests that read patches. Expect a new order in patch snapshots, and copy a patch value before changing it. See Patches.
  4. Review code that relies on auto-freeze. Frozen Maps and Sets no longer accept new properties or replaced methods, and a returned value must not hold drafts inside frozen objects. See Returned values.
  5. Respect draft lifetimes. Consume value-producing iterators while their draft is active, and use original(draft), current(draft) or an id rather than a draft as a Map key. A Set subclass's add() must store the value it receives; see collection lifetimes.
  6. Check arrays with getters on their indices, which the native methods read as plain values. See Arrays.
  7. Type-check your code, and revisit casts that worked around the async and apply() types of 1.x. The declarations support TypeScript 5.0 and later. See TypeScript.
  8. Recheck tests that pin results of 1.x, especially for Sets, patches, apply() and current(): the new result may be the intended one. See Fixes that change results.

Coming from Immer

Mutative passes Immer's test suite, adapted to its API, and most Immer code moves over by renaming: produce() becomes create(), produceWithPatches() becomes create() with enablePatches: true, applyPatches() becomes apply(), and nothing becomes rawReturn(undefined). Drop the plugin calls, since Mutative has no plugins, and replace [immerable] with a mark. The main decision is freezing: Immer freezes the next state by default and Mutative does not, so set enableAutoFreeze: true, for example with makeCreator(), if your code relies on frozen state. The migration guide from Immer walks through each step, Comparison with Immer lists every difference, checked against Immer 11.1.18, and mutative-compat wraps Mutative in Immer's API for a quicker switch; at the time of writing, it declares Mutative 1.x as its peer dependency.

Thanks

Thanks to everyone who reported issues, reviewed changes and built libraries on Mutative. The docs were revised alongside 2.0: their code examples run as tests of the library, and new guides cover pitfalls and performance tips. If something behaves differently after you upgrade, or the migration guide misses a case, please open an issue or start a discussion.

articles.title: Your Tabs Each Open Their Own WebSocket. navigator.locks Elects One.
articles.description: Six open tabs means six live connections to your server, six duplicate pushes, six timers draining the battery. navigator.locks elects a single leader tab to hold the real connection — the rest just listen.
articles.body_html:
Open your app in six tabs — most people have at least that many of something open right now — and check your server's connection count. If you're using WebSockets or Server-Sent Events for live updates, it just went up by six. Six sockets, six keep-alives, six copies of every push notification landing in the same browser window.

Nobody asked for six connections. They asked to see their dashboard update live. You gave them that, and also a server bill and a battery drain that scale with how many tabs a bookmark-happy user happens to have open.

The bug you can see in your own network tab

Open devtools, go to the Network tab, filter by WS, and open the same page twice. You'll see two independent socket connections, each sending its own ping, each receiving its own copy of every broadcast the server sends.

Now open six. Your server — which probably caps concurrent connections per deploy, or bills per connection-minute — just got six times the load from one human being. And when the server pushes a notification, that human sees it pop up six times, once per tab, because each tab's JavaScript has no idea the other five exist.

The fix that doesn't fix it

The obvious instinct is the Page Visibility API: pause the connection in background tabs, since the user is only looking at one of them anyway.

document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => {
  if (document.hidden) socket.close();
  else socket = new WebSocket(url);
});

This helps a little and breaks something else. A user with the dashboard open on a second monitor, in a visible-but-not-active tab, stops getting updates. Worse, "hidden" and "pointless" aren't the same thing — a background tab doing the actual relaying for a visible one is exactly what you want, not what you're trying to kill.

The real problem was never "which tabs should connect." It's that six tabs are duplicating work that only needs to happen once. You don't want fewer connections scattered unpredictably across whichever tabs happen to be visible — you want exactly one connection, owned by exactly one tab, with the other five just listening in.

That's leader election, and the browser already ships the primitive for it.

navigator.locks, held for the life of a tab

navigator.locks.request() normally looks like a mutex: acquire a named lock, do some work, let it resolve, the lock releases. But nothing requires the callback to resolve quickly. Give it a promise that never resolves on its own, and the lock stays held for as long as that tab is open — the moment the tab closes, crashes, or navigates away, the browser releases the lock for you, automatically, no cleanup code required.

That's the whole mechanism. Whichever tab's request() call wins the (exclusive, FIFO) queue becomes the leader. Every other tab's request just waits — and the instant the leader's tab closes, the next one in line is granted the lock and takes over.

const LEADER_LOCK = 'app-connection-leader';
let socket;

navigator.locks.request(LEADER_LOCK, () => {
  // Only one tab's callback ever runs this at a time.
  socket = new WebSocket('wss://example.com/live');
  socket.onmessage = (e) => {
    channel.postMessage({ tick: e.data }); // fan out to every other tab
    renderUpdate(e.data);                  // and render here too — see why below
  };

  return new Promise(() => {}); // never resolves — holds the lock until this tab dies
});

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Relaying to the followers

Electing a leader only solves half the problem — the other five tabs still need the updates. That's what BroadcastChannel is for: the leader relays every message it receives onto a channel that every other tab is already listening to.

const channel = new BroadcastChannel('app-updates');

// Every follower tab runs this:
channel.onmessage = (e) => renderUpdate(e.data.tick);

Here's the gotcha worth knowing before you build this: a BroadcastChannel never delivers a message back to the instance that posted it — that's by design, not a bug. So the leader can't just post to the channel and expect its own onmessage to fire; that's why the leader's socket.onmessage above renders directly instead of waiting for an echo that will never arrive. Followers never touch the real connection — they only ever get updates through the channel. If a follower needs to send something back (a user action, a form submit), it posts that onto the channel too, and the leader is the only one that forwards it to the server. One tab talks to your backend. The rest just listen.

What happens when the leader closes

This is the part worth testing yourself, because it's the part that makes this worth doing at all: close the leader tab, and one of the waiting tabs is granted the lock as soon as the browser notices that tab's context is gone — no polling, no "is anyone still there" timeout, no stale leader lingering for thirty seconds before a new one takes over. The browser's lock queue is the failover mechanism — you don't write one.

There's a brief gap you should know about: the new leader has to open its own WebSocket connection after acquiring the lock, so there's a reconnect delay (normal connection-establishment time) before live updates resume. For a dashboard or notification feed, that's invisible. For something that can't tolerate a gap at all, keep that in mind rather than assuming the handoff is instant.

One more option worth knowing: navigator.locks.request(name, { ifAvailable: true }, callback) checks leadership without joining the queue — callback runs immediately with null if someone else already holds the lock, instead of waiting. Useful for a tab that wants to know "am I the leader?" without volunteering to become one.

Try it with real tabs, not a mental model

Everything above is easy to agree with and easy to get wrong in practice — the FIFO ordering, the automatic release, the reconnect gap. The playground above runs the exact same navigator.locks + BroadcastChannel code in three simulated tabs on one page. Open each one, watch the lock queue hand off leadership the moment you close the leader, and try the "steal" option to see what happens when a tab forces its way to the front instead of waiting in line.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

Browser support, honestly

navigator.locks is Baseline widely available — Chrome 69+, Firefox 96+, Safari 15.4+ — so this works in every current browser. The one footgun is the steal option: it forcibly yanks the lock away from whoever holds it, skipping the queue entirely. That's occasionally the right tool (a user force-reloading a stuck tab), but use it knowing the previous leader never gets a chance to finish cleanly — it just loses the lock mid-flight.

You don't need six tabs each holding their own connection to do the job of one. You need one tab doing the job, and a browser API that already knows how to pick which one — and hand the job to the next tab the moment the first one leaves.

Does your app open a connection per tab right now? Go count it in the Network panel — I'll bet it's more than you think.

📚 Read next

  • Stop using the localStorage hack to sync browser tabs. BroadcastChannel does it natively.
  • Five tabs open, one refresh token — the race nobody noticed
