articles.title: Five small free apps: your voice, your birthday, your song, your photo, and a bedtime story
articles.description: August was for websites. September was for music videos. October finally belonged to the small apps:...
articles.body_html:
August was for websites. September was for music videos. October finally belonged to the small apps: ideas that had been spinning around in my head for a while, waiting for their turn. This month they got built.

The first four share one rule: everything you see and hear comes from what you give them. Your voice, your name and birth date, your song, your photo. Nothing is random and nothing is picked from a library, so the same input always gives the same result. The fifth is a small gift for anyone with little kids.

All five are free and run entirely in the browser. No account, no server, and nothing you record, type or upload ever leaves your device. Videos are rendered frame by frame and encoded straight to MP4, not recorded from the screen, so they don't stutter and open on any phone.

They all live on one small site: My Little Apps | Kuga Lab, https://mylittleapps.pages.dev

1. Rosonata: say your name, get a rosette that plays music

Say your name into the microphone. Two seconds later you have a glowing rosette with petals, rings and little gold spikes. Press Play, and a needle starts reading it like a music box, while a real piano (or a harp, a cello and a French horn) plays what it finds.

Where it came from

Before Rosonata there was a simpler app: say a name, get a mandala-like rosette, with one strict rule that everything must come from the voice. Looking at one of those rosettes, it suddenly looked like the disc from an old music box: rings, bumps, a steady rhythm around the circle. It looked like a score. So the question became: what if the rosette could sing?

Listening to the voice

The recording is cut into short overlapping frames, and for each one the app measures loudness, pitch, brightness, 12 frequency bands, and how often the wave crosses zero, which is how it finds hissing sounds like s, sh and ch. Silence is trimmed, and the loudness peaks split the name into syllables.

Drawing the rosette

Every measurement has one job:

  1. the median pitch of the voice sets the number of arms (10 to 18) and the base colour
  2. every syllable becomes a ring
  3. the pitch and loudness of that syllable shape the petals in its ring
  4. hissing sounds become spikes, loud moments become dots
  5. a medallion in the centre sums up the whole name

The number of arms is one line. pc is where the voice falls inside an octave (0 to 11):

const N = Math.round(14 - 4 * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * pc / 12)); // 10..18 arms

It goes around the octave like a circle instead of up a ladder, so low voices don't always get fewer arms. A deep voice and a high voice can both land on 18.

Reading it like a music box

As the disc turns, wherever a petal line crosses the needle, a note sounds. Further from the centre means higher. To keep it from sounding like a cat on a keyboard, every note snaps to a pentatonic scale in the key of the voice that said the name:

const PENT = [0, 2, 4, 7, 9];
const deg2semi = d => 12 * Math.floor(d / 5) + PENT[((d % 5) + 5) % 5];
let key = 57 + Math.round(pc); // the key comes from your voice

There are two ways to read. Classic: the needle stands still, the medallion gives the bass, and on the last arm the disc slows down like a music box running out of spring. Complex: the needle travels from the centre to the edge like a gramophone, the dots and spikes set the rhythm, and every phrase reads a different line.

The sound comes from real recorded instruments (tonejs-instruments). There are three sounds: Piano, Salon (piano, harp, cello) and Film (French horn, harp, piano, cello), all through a concert-hall reverb. You can keep the rosette as a PNG, a 1080×1080 MP4 or a WAV.

The detours

The first version had no instruments at all. You recorded your name, then sang "laaa", and your own voice became a choir. It crackled, for three reasons. The click or breath at the start of the recording was replayed on every note. A deep voice pushed two octaves up sounded like broken glass. And the phone simply couldn't mix dozens of voices live: the exported WAV was clean, but live playback crackled. The fix for that last one stayed in the app. The whole piece is rendered offline first, and only one finished buffer is played:

const oc = new OfflineAudioContext(2, Math.ceil(seconds * 44100), 44100);
// ...schedule every note into oc...
const buffer = await oc.startRendering(); // then play just this

It hasn't crackled since, even on a mid-range Android phone.

The next discovery: every melody went up, down, up. Of course, because petals go out and come back. So came other paths through the rosette: a golden spiral, a nautilus (which, by the way, is not a golden spiral, that's a popular myth), sunflower seeds at 137.5°, Archimedes' spiral, a rose curve, Lissajous figures. At one point there were about twelve reading modes and six instruments.

A scoring function then measured which option was the most "melodic". On paper, the spirals won. To the ear, plain piano going up and down sounded best, and the violin was shrieking. And a visitor who sees fifteen buttons just leaves. So the extra code was removed, not hidden, and the best ideas from the experiments were folded into Complex.

Try it: https://mylittleapps.pages.dev/rosonata/app

2. Melodentity: your name and birthday as a melody nobody else has

It started with a claim seen online: if you match name and birth time down to the minute, only 1 to 5 people in the world share yours, even for the most common names.

It's wrong. About 250 babies are born every minute worldwide. The most common full name on Earth, Wang Wei, belongs to roughly 290,000 people. Spread over about 70 years of birthdays, that's around 10 per calendar date, and divided by the 1,440 minutes in a day, 0.007 Wang Weis per minute. The "1 to 5" only appears if you forget the birth year.

So for almost everyone alive, name + date + time of birth is already unique. Which means it could become something that belongs to only one person: a melody.

You type your full name, in any alphabet, your date and your time of birth. You get a short tune with a synth or a real grand piano, the same tune as real piano sheet music, and a PNG of the score and an MP3 of the melody. Change one letter or one minute and you get a completely different tune.

Version 1, and how it broke

The first version mapped things directly: each digit of the date became a melody note, each letter of the name an accompaniment note, the time of birth set the tempo. It sounded nice and felt unique. Then came the question: can two people get the same tune? The math said yes, in several ways:

  1. Only the first 5 letters were heard, so Marko Petrović and Marko Jovanović sounded identical.
  2. The note was charCode % 10, so A, K and U shared a note. Nina = Dina, Hana = Rana.
  3. Tempo depended on the distance from noon, so 10:00 and 14:00 sounded the same.
  4. Cyrillic letters were silently deleted, so every name written in Cyrillic got no accompaniment.

Patching each hole would only patch the holes found so far.

Version 2: a fingerprint

Name, date and time are joined into one string and run through SHA-256. The result is a 256-bit fingerprint, and changing a single character changes the whole thing. Every musical decision is then read from that number, one after another:

// each choice "uses up" part of the fingerprint
function hashReader(hex){
  let big = BigInt('0x' + hex);
  return n => {
    const N = BigInt(n);
    const r = Number(big % N);
    big /= N;
    return r;
  };
}

const R = hashReader(sha256(`${name} | ${date} | ${time}`));
const tempo = BPMS[R(8)];         // one of 8 tempos
const pitch = PENT8[R(8)];        // one of 8 notes
const length = DURATIONS[R(3)];   // short, long, or short + rest

Every letter counts, every alphabet works, and there are no symmetries. Before hashing, the name is normalized: upper and lower case are the same, extra spaces don't count, and Ана Петровић = Ana Petrović, because it's the same person in two scripts. But č is not c: Petrović and Petrovic are spelled differently.

Two modes

In Date + fingerprint mode, the melody is your birth date, one note per digit, so you can actually hear your birthday. The accompaniment comes from the fingerprint and tells apart the roughly 360,000 people born that day. It has 16 notes, because that's where the chance of two people sharing a tune drops below one in a million, and 8 digits × 2 eighth notes fill the bar exactly. In Pure fingerprint mode, 24 melody notes come from the fingerprint of everything, over 4 slow bass notes. An honest caveat: a hash makes uniqueness overwhelmingly likely, not mathematically guaranteed.

Sheet music a pianist can play

The score is drawn with VexFlow as a grand staff. A phrase can be 9, 10, 11 or 12 eighth notes long, so instead of forcing it into 4/4, each bar gets its true time signature: 11/8, 9/8. Long bass notes are written with ties, short notes get staccato dots, accented notes get accent marks. 120 combinations were checked in both modes: every note on paper starts and ends exactly where the sound does.

The piano uses 12 recordings from the Salamander Grand Piano. The MP3 uses the same offline rendering as Rosonata, encoded in the browser with lamejs.

The rule that caught the Nina = Dina problem: agree first, code second. The first version felt unique. Only "prove that two people can't get the same tune" showed the holes.

Try it: https://mylittleapps.pages.dev/melodentity/app

3. Songlyph: 25 visualizer experiments, one app

After a month of making music videos in code, the phone was full of experiments with names like tacke-v11-2.html and linija-v4-1.html. About 25 files, many of them slightly different versions of the same idea. Four ideas survived:

  1. Line: a line that wanders, spirals or writes rows across the canvas, steered by the song.
  2. Dots: discs that fall on every beat and fill the canvas as the song goes.
  3. Circle of fifths: the harmony of the song drawn as a path around the circle of fifths, with rings and chord lines on each beat.
  4. Signature: a line whose whole behaviour comes from a few numbers measured from the entire song.

Instead of four apps, there's one, with a Layers switch that stacks several modes on the same canvas. That's Songlyph: song + glyph.

You upload any song, and the app first listens to all of it: tempo and beats, chords, loudness, bass and treble, stereo width, and the points where the song changes parts. Then it draws while the song plays, and every trait leaves its own trace. Beats drop shapes, chords pick the colour and the direction, loudness sets size and brightness, stereo width splits the line in two, and new parts of the song leave rings. You can save a full-resolution PNG, or a video with the song in 1:1, 9:16 or 16:9.

There are a lot of switches: four modes with their own options, layers, six palettes, a dark or light canvas, bokeh lights, "breathing", a seed and a manual tempo fix. If you like visualizers, drop in a song you love and play. If you write code, open the source: one HTML file, a hand-written FFT and beat detection, no frameworks. Change a number and you get a different drawing. Take it apart.

Try it: https://mylittleapps.pages.dev/songlyph/app

4. Kaleidosong: the kaleidoscope, back where it belongs

Almost everyone had one as a kid. A cardboard tube, a few pieces of coloured glass, three little mirrors. You held it up to the light, turned it slowly, and a new pattern bloomed every second. Nobody had to explain it, and nobody owned it. It was the cheapest toy in the shop, and every child in the world got to hold one.

So it was strange to find kaleidoscope apps that charge for HD, for a longer video, or to remove a watermark.

Kaleidosong is free. Give it one picture and one song, and it turns them into a living kaleidoscope that moves with the music: squares like mirrored tiles, or hexagons, exactly like three mirrors in a tube. No account, no watermark, no limit. Take a photo of your street, your cat, your grandmother's tablecloth, put your favourite song under it, and turn the tube.

Try it: https://mylittleapps.pages.dev/kaleidosong/app

5. Storyglobe: four picture books, free for every child

This one is a small present for everyone with little kids at home.

Four picture books, each with a gentle lesson, illustrations and a little song at the end:

  1. Lioner Learns to Stay Safe
  2. Greenosaur Learns to Brush His Teeth
  3. Foxin Learns to Share
  4. Owlo, a little owl who doesn't want to go to bed

Read them together on the screen, in your own language, or download them and keep them. No account, no ads, no price. Good stories for kids should be free, just like the kaleidoscope.

Read them: https://mylittleapps.pages.dev/storyglobe/

If you try any of them, show what you got in the comments: your rosette, your tune, your drawing, your kaleidoscope. And if you read a book with your kid, tell me if I made some mistakes in your mother's language 🙂

Credits: piano samples from the Salamander Grand Piano by Alexander Holm (CC BY 3.0). Instrument samples from tonejs-instruments, VSCO 2 Community Orchestra and Freesound (CC BY 3.0). Sheet music by VexFlow (MIT). MP3 encoding by lamejs (LGPL-3.0). Video export with mp4-muxer (MIT).

All five apps were built on a phone, in conversation with Claude. This post was written with help from AI.

Cheers 🥂

articles.title: Running OCR entirely in the browser (and making scanned PDFs editable)
articles.description: A few months ago I needed to change one line in a scanned contract. Every "free" PDF site I tried...
articles.body_html:
A few months ago I needed to change one line in a scanned contract. Every "free" PDF site I tried wanted me to upload the file to their server first. One let me edit for ten minutes and then asked me to pay to download the result.

That's a strange deal for a contract, a passport scan or a payslip. So I started building PDFkind, a PDF editor where everything happens in the browser. The hardest part by far was OCR: reading the text out of a scan, then turning it into real text you can edit.

This post is about how that works, what broke along the way, and the numbers I got. Everything runs client-side; the server only hands out static files.

The constraint: no server, no exceptions

The rule I set myself was simple: the document never leaves the device. No "we delete it after an hour", no API call to a cloud OCR service. That rules out the easy options and leaves two questions:

  1. Which OCR engine can run in a browser tab with acceptable quality?
  2. How big a download can I ask people to accept?

First try: Tesseract.js

Tesseract.js is the obvious choice. It's mature, easy to use, and works well on clean scans. On my test set it was fine for flat, well-lit documents.

Then I tried phone photos: slightly tilted pages, shadows, uneven lighting. That's what people actually have when they "scan" something. Tesseract mostly fell apart:

Document type Tesseract.js PaddleOCR (what I ended up with)
Poor-quality scans 3.5 to 6.4% of characters wrong about 1%
Phone photos unusable 10 to 14%

(Character error rate on my own small test set of French and English documents. Not a benchmark, but the gap was big enough to decide.)

The difference comes from how the text is found. Tesseract relies on classical layout analysis, which struggles once the page isn't flat and evenly lit. PaddleOCR uses a neural network to find text lines first, and that detector copes much better with real-world photos.

PaddleOCR in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web

PaddleOCR is normally a Python library, but its models can be exported to ONNX and run with onnxruntime-web in WebAssembly. I use the PP-OCRv5 mobile models:

  • a detection model that finds text lines
  • a recognition model for Latin-script languages (English, French, Spanish, German and so on)

Together with the WASM runtime that's about 20 MB. It's only downloaded the first time someone uses OCR, and it's cached for 30 days:

// next.config.ts
async headers() {
  return [{
    source: '/ocr/:file*',
    headers: [{ key: 'Cache-Control', value: 'public, max-age=2592000, stale-while-revalidate=86400' }],
  }];
}

One setting worth knowing about: I run ONNX Runtime with numThreads = 1. Multi-threaded WASM needs SharedArrayBuffer, which in turn needs the page to be cross-origin isolated (COOP/COEP headers). Those headers break a lot of third-party embeds. One thread is slower, but a page of OCR still takes a few seconds, which is fine.

OCR happens in two steps: find the lines, then read each line.

Step 1: finding the text lines

The detector (a DBNet model) takes the page image and returns a probability map: for every pixel, how likely it is to be text.

Preparing the input has a couple of traps. The image size must be a multiple of 32, and PaddleOCR models expect BGR channel order, not RGB, normalized with the ImageNet mean and standard deviation:

const MEAN = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406], STD = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225];
// resize so the longest side is at most 1600 px, rounded to multiples of 32
const k = Math.min(1, 1600 / Math.max(canvas.width, canvas.height));
const W = Math.max(32, Math.round((canvas.width * k) / 32) * 32);
const H = Math.max(32, Math.round((canvas.height * k) / 32) * 32);

const px = getPixels(canvas, W, H); // RGBA from a resized canvas
const plane = W * H, input = new Float32Array(3 * plane);
for (let i = 0, p = 0; p < plane; i += 4, p++) {
  input[p]             = (px[i + 2] / 255 - MEAN[0]) / STD[0]; // B
  input[plane + p]     = (px[i + 1] / 255 - MEAN[1]) / STD[1]; // G
  input[2 * plane + p] = (px[i]     / 255 - MEAN[2]) / STD[2]; // R
}
const out = await session.run({ [session.inputNames[0]]: new ort.Tensor('float32', input, [1, 3, H, W]) });

The probability map isn't a list of boxes yet. Turning it into lines is the post-processing that the Python library normally does for you, so I had to rewrite it in TypeScript:

  1. Threshold the map (pixels above 0.3 count as text).
  2. Flood fill to group connected text pixels into regions.
  3. Drop regions that are too small or whose average score is below 0.6.
  4. Compute each region's convex hull, then the minimum-area rotated rectangle around it. This is what makes tilted lines work.
  5. Expand ("unclip") the rectangle, because the model predicts a slightly shrunk core of each line.

The expansion distance comes from the DBNet paper: area × ratio ÷ perimeter.

const d = (r.w * r.h * UNCLIP) / (2 * (r.w + r.h)); // UNCLIP = 1.6
const w = r.w + 2 * d, h = r.h + 2 * d;

The bug that cost me a day: my first version found the four corners of each box by sorting them by y coordinate. That works on a flat scan. On a tilted photo, the top-right corner of a line can be lower than its bottom-left corner, so lines got read upside down or mirrored. Recognition on photos was garbage and I couldn't figure out why.

The fix was to stop guessing corners from coordinates and derive them from the rectangle's angle instead. I keep the angle within ±45° (swapping width and height when needed), so the width always runs along the text line. Then the corners come out in a known order: top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left.

Step 2: reading each line

The recognizer expects one straight, horizontal strip of text, 48 pixels high. So each detected line, which may be tilted, has to be cut out and straightened.

Canvas can do this with a single affine transform. Map three corners of the detected box to the corners of the output strip, invert the matrix, and draw the page through it:

function crop(src: HTMLCanvasElement, quad: [number, number][], boxW: number, boxH: number, outH = 48) {
  const w = Math.max(8, Math.round((boxW / boxH) * outH)), h = outH;
  const c = document.createElement('canvas');
  c.width = w; c.height = h;
  const g = c.getContext('2d')!;
  const [p0, p1, , p3] = quad; // top-left, top-right, bottom-left
  // matrix mapping strip coordinates to page coordinates...
  const a = (p1[0] - p0[0]) / w, b = (p1[1] - p0[1]) / w;
  const cc = (p3[0] - p0[0]) / h, d = (p3[1] - p0[1]) / h;
  // ...inverted, so drawing the page lands the line flat in the strip
  const det = a * d - b * cc;
  const ia = d / det, ib = -b / det, ic = -cc / det, id = a / det;
  g.setTransform(ia, ib, ic, id, -(ia * p0[0] + ic * p0[1]), -(ib * p0[0] + id * p0[1]));
  g.drawImage(src, 0, 0);
  return g.getImageData(0, 0, w, h);
}

The recognizer outputs, for each horizontal position in the strip, a probability for every character in its dictionary. Turning that into text is CTC greedy decoding: take the most likely character at each step, merge repeats, drop the "blank" symbol.

// dictionary: blank first, space last (PaddleOCR convention)
const dict = ['', ...chars, ' '];
let text = '', prev = -1, conf = 0, n = 0;
for (let t = 0; t < steps; t++) {
  let best = 0, max = -Infinity;
  for (let k = 0; k < classes; k++) {
    const v = out[t * classes + k];
    if (v > max) { max = v; best = k; }
  }
  if (best !== 0 && best !== prev) { text += dict[best]; conf += max; n++; }
  prev = best;
}

The average probability of the kept characters gives a confidence score. I skip lines below 0.4: they're usually logos, stamps or noise.

Arabic needed a different approach

I'm from Morocco, and a lot of documents here mix French and Arabic, sometimes in the same line. PaddleOCR's Arabic recognizer was disappointing in my tests: it dropped digits and letters often enough to be useless for things like dates and ID numbers.

What worked was a hybrid:

  • keep PaddleOCR's detector to find the lines, since it's robust to photos
  • read Arabic lines with Tesseract in single-line mode, on a cleaned-up crop of each line

The cleanup makes a big difference with Tesseract. For each line strip I estimate the background with a max filter (the paper is the brightest thing around), blur it, divide the image by it to flatten shadows and uneven light, then stretch the contrast between two percentiles. Tesseract then sees near-black text on near-white paper.

Two more details:

  • Line joining. The detector often splits a line at wide gaps, for example after a colon. For Arabic I join pieces that sit on the same row and are close together (gap under 2.5× the line height), then order them right to left. The gap limit matters: without it, a French heading on the left and an Arabic heading on the right got merged into one nonsense line.
  • A Tesseract setting that silently drops spaces. I had preserve_interword_spaces: '1' enabled. On Arabic it removed the spaces between words entirely ("شهادةعمل" instead of "شهادة عمل"). Turning it off fixed it. If your Arabic OCR output has words glued together, check this first.

On my Arabic test documents the hybrid gets about 2 to 4% of characters wrong on scans and around 4% on phone photos. Not perfect, but very usable.

From "searchable" to "editable"

Recognizing text is half the job. The classic output of OCR is a searchable PDF: the recognized text is added as an invisible layer behind the image, so you can select and copy it while the page looks unchanged.

That's useful, but it doesn't answer the question people actually ask: "how do I change the text in my scan?" So the editor has an option to go further. Each recognized line gets:

  1. a cover in the color of the paper, hiding the original pixels
  2. a real text box on top, with the same words, roughly the same font, size, weight, slant and ink color

Getting that to look right is mostly careful measuring.

Paper and ink color. The paper color is the most common color along the edges of the line strip (bucketed to 5 bits per channel so noise doesn't matter). The ink color is the average of the darkest pixels inside the letters. Edge pixels blend with the paper, so averaging all of them would make the text look washed out.

Font size. I measure the height of the ink from the top of the letters to the baseline, then ask the browser how tall the same text is in a candidate font:

ctx.font = `100px ${family}`;
const m = ctx.measureText(text);
const size = inkHeightAboveBaseline / (m.actualBoundingBoxAscent / 100);

Using actualBoundingBoxAscent for the exact text matters. A line with no capitals or tall letters ("one more") is shorter than "Total", and a fixed cap-height ratio gets the size wrong.

Which font? I can't identify arbitrary typefaces, but I can tell serif from sans serif. For each candidate (Helvetica, Times), I draw the recognized text into an offscreen canvas, stretched to the same length as the original, and measure how well it overlaps the original's letter shapes (intersection over union). The best overlap wins. Since a page is usually set in one typeface, a family that clearly wins most lines also gets a bonus on close calls.

Bold. My first attempt compared stroke thickness, and it failed on blurry scans, where everything looks bold. What works is comparing the total amount of ink in a line with how much ink the regular-weight font would use for the same text. Blur spreads ink out but doesn't change the total. And because a faded scan affects every line alike, I compare each line with the page's median rather than an absolute threshold.

Italic. I shear the letter shapes by different amounts and keep the shear at which the vertical strokes line up best (the sum of squared column counts peaks). Upright text peaks at 0; italic peaks at around 0.1 to 0.25.

Width. Finally, a little letter spacing makes the new text exactly as long as the original, so it doesn't overlap whatever comes after it.

The result isn't pixel-perfect. Unusual fonts come out as Helvetica or Times, and handwriting is left alone. But for the common case (fix a date, a name, an amount on a scanned letter) it's close enough that the change is hard to spot.

What I'd tell someone trying this

  • Test on phone photos early. Clean scans hide almost every problem.
  • ONNX Runtime Web is production-ready, but you have to rewrite the pre- and post-processing that Python libraries normally hide. Budget time for it.
  • Cache the models aggressively and load them only when the feature is used. Nobody should download 20 MB just to merge two PDFs.
  • Measure with real documents and track a simple error rate. Several of my "obvious" improvements made things worse.

Try it

Everything above is live in PDFkind. It's free, with no signup. Open a scanned PDF in the editor, tick "Make scanned text editable", and you can check in DevTools that your file never goes over the network.

I'd love feedback, especially from anyone who has worked on OCR or PDF internals. Where does it break for you?

articles.title: How to migrate Pipedream workflows to n8n before the March 2027 shutdown
articles.description: Pipedream Workflows and String stop running on March 31, 2027. All Workflows data, including...
articles.body_html:
Pipedream Workflows and String stop running on March 31, 2027. All Workflows data, including connected accounts and their OAuth tokens, is deleted by April 30, 2027. Pipedream Connect is not affected.

Neither Pipedream nor n8n offers an importer, so moving to n8n means rebuilding each workflow in n8n's own format. Most of it is mechanical once you know the equivalents. This post covers the equivalents, the parts that break, and an order of work.

1. Get your workflows out

You have three ways to get workflow definitions:

  • The official export. In a project, open Settings and click Export Workflows. Pipedream writes a ZIP to the project's File Store: a manifest.json plus one JSON file per workflow, with triggers, steps, code, props and branches. Pipedream's docs say File Stores are an Advanced-plan feature, so on Free or Basic the button may not work.
  • GitHub Sync. If a project was ever synced, the repository has a workflow.yaml per workflow and a file per code step.
  • The REST API. GET https://api.pipedream.com/v1/workflows/{id}?org_id=o_xxx with an API key returns a workflow's definition. It isn't confirmed on Free or Basic plans, so try one workflow first.

Whatever you use, some things never come out:

  • secret values, which are exported as <redacted>;
  • OAuth tokens, which become just an account ID;
  • environment variable values;
  • data store records and File Store files;
  • event history;
  • the code of private components.

Read manifest.json first: its warnings list names every redacted prop. One export holds at most 500 workflows or 256 MB.

Save a few real sample events from each workflow now. On Free and Basic, Pipedream keeps only the last 100 events or 7 days. You'll want them to test the n8n version.

2. Choose n8n Cloud or self-hosted

This choice depends mostly on your code steps:

  • n8n Cloud. The Code node can load only crypto and moment in JavaScript. Python steps can't import anything at all.
  • Self-hosted n8n. Set NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL=axios,lodash (and NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN for Node's own modules), and install the packages where the task runner can load them.

If most of your imports are HTTP clients and date libraries, Cloud is fine: HTTP calls can use this.helpers.httpRequest() inside the Code node, and Luxon is built in. If you depend on SDKs or Python libraries, self-hosting saves a lot of rewriting.

3. Map the triggers

Pipedream n8n
HTTP / webhook trigger Webhook node
$.respond() in a step Respond to Webhook node, with the Webhook node's Respond option set to "Using 'Respond to Webhook' Node"
Schedule (cron or interval) Schedule Trigger
App event (new row, new email…) The app's n8n trigger node, if it exists

Three things bite here:

  • Webhook URLs change. Every service that calls your *.m.pipedream.net URL needs the new n8n production URL.
  • Some intervals don't fit one rule. n8n's interval rules count seconds up to 59, minutes up to 59, hours up to 23 and days up to 31. "Every 90 minutes" becomes two cron rules: 0 0,3,6,9,12,15,18,21 * * * and 30 1,4,7,10,13,16,19,22 * * *.
  • Polling triggers batch items. Pipedream ran your workflow once per new row or email. n8n's polling triggers (Google Sheets, Gmail, Airtable…) return every new item in one execution. Code written for a single event quietly processes only the first one. Either put Loop Over Items after the trigger and call the rest of the flow with Execute Workflow per item, or rewrite the code for $input.all().

4. Map steps and branches

Pipedream n8n
Registry action (Slack, Google Sheets…) The app's n8n node, or HTTP Request
If/else block If node (one condition branch) or Switch node (several)
Switch block Switch node in Rules mode
Filter step, $.flow.exit() If node with nothing connected to the branch that stops
Delay Wait node
Parallel block Branches from one node, then a Merge node
Loop block Loop Over Items

One difference changes results silently: Pipedream's rule builder compares text without regard to case, and n8n's If node is case-sensitive unless you turn on its Ignore Case option.

Steps after a Pipedream block read steps.<block>.$return_value, the result of whichever branch ran. In n8n, add a node where the branches meet and point later expressions at it.

Prop expressions change syntax too: {{steps.trigger.event.body.email}} becomes {{ $('trigger').first().json.body.email }}. Name your n8n nodes after the old step names and most references translate one to one.

5. Convert the code steps

A Pipedream Node.js step:

import axios from "axios";

export default defineComponent({
  async run({ steps, $ }) {
    const email = steps.trigger.event.body.email;
    const { data } = await axios.get("https://api.example.com/users", { params: { email } });
    if (!data.active) return $.flow.exit("inactive user");
    $.export("userId", data.id);
    return data;
  },
});

The same logic in an n8n Code node ("Run Once for All Items", with the Webhook node named trigger):

const email = $('trigger').first().json.body.email;
const data = await this.helpers.httpRequest({
  method: 'GET',
  url: 'https://api.example.com/users',
  qs: { email },
  json: true,
});

// Like $.flow.exit(): no items out, so nothing after this node runs.
if (!data.active) return [];

return [{ json: { ...data, userId: data.id } }];

The rules behind it:

  • steps.x.$return_value becomes $('x').first().json.
  • $.export() and the return value become fields of the items you return. n8n items are always objects, so wrap a string or an array.
  • $.flow.exit() becomes return [].
  • axios, got and node-fetch become this.helpers.httpRequest(), which works on n8n Cloud.
  • Pipedream data stores become workflow static data ($getWorkflowStaticData('global')) or n8n Data tables. Static data is only saved for published workflows started by a trigger, not for manual test runs.
  • Code nodes can't read n8n credentials by design. If a step used this.someApp.$auth, move that API call into an HTTP Request node that uses an n8n credential.

6. Credentials, secrets and variables

  1. Create an n8n credential for every connected account and select it on the matching nodes.
  2. Re-enter redacted secrets in credentials, or as n8n Variables. Variables are available on n8n Cloud Pro and Enterprise and on self-hosted Business and Enterprise.
  3. Since n8n 2.0, N8N_BLOCK_ENV_ACCESS_IN_NODE defaults to true, so Code nodes can't read environment variables unless you change it on a self-hosted instance.

7. Import, test and cut over

  1. Import each workflow JSON from the editor (workflow menu, Import from File), or in bulk with the public API: POST /api/v1/workflows with an X-N8N-API-KEY header. The API isn't available on the Cloud free trial.
  2. Imported workflows start unpublished. In n8n 2.x you publish a workflow instead of toggling it active.
  3. Replay your saved sample events and compare the outputs with Pipedream's.
  4. Point each webhook sender at the new production URL. Watch the Executions list for a few days, then turn the Pipedream workflow off.
  5. Copy data store records and File Store files out before April 30, 2027.

Start with the workflows that have the most outside dependencies (webhook senders, OAuth apps), because those take the longest to switch. If you're stuck on a specific Pipedream pattern, ask in the comments.

This article was written with the help of AI. The mappings and the code example were checked against Pipedream workflows converted and run in n8n 2.x.

articles.title: Testing WebRTC without a camera: a loopback self-test that proves the whole path
articles.description: The hardest part of testing a WebRTC pipeline is that the real one needs a camera, a microphone, a...
articles.body_html:
The hardest part of testing a WebRTC pipeline is that the real one needs a camera, a microphone, a user who clicks allow, and HTTPS. On a build machine none of that exists, so the pipeline tests get skipped and the first honest test is a human on a laptop.

There is a better fixture. Put a canvas on one end and a <video> element on the other, and send the canvas through the actual stack — publisher, signaling, SFU, viewer — so what the test exercises is the real path and not a mock.

The whole thing in one line: a canvas is an acceptable substitute for a camera, a timer is a better driver than an animation frame, and a moving timestamp is what proves the picture is live rather than merely present.

Replace the camera with a canvas

canvas.captureStream() returns a MediaStream with the same shape as a camera's, so everything downstream is unchanged:

const stream = cv.captureStream(30);
for (const track of stream.getVideoTracks()) {
  pc.addTrack(track, stream);
}

No permission prompt, no device enumeration, no browser variation in which camera it picked. The test runs headless, on a server, in CI, and on a machine whose only camera is already in use by a call.

Draw something that can only be live

A static image is a trap. If the encoder dies and the last frame stays on screen, a static test pattern passes. Draw motion and a clock:

function draw() {
  const t = performance.now();
  ctx.fillStyle = '#101418';
  ctx.fillRect(0, 0, cv.width, cv.height);

  const x = ((t / 8) % (cv.width + 80)) - 80;   // a moving block
  ctx.fillStyle = '#5b8cff';
  ctx.fillRect(x, 120, 80, 80);

  ctx.fillStyle = '#e6e9ef';
  ctx.font = '20px monospace';
  ctx.fillText(new Date().toLocaleTimeString() + '.' + String(Math.floor(t % 1000)).padStart(3, '0'), 16, 34);
}

The timestamp is the assertion. A frozen stream shows a stopped clock, and a stream that is alive shows a clock that keeps moving, so the test can tell "connected and carrying video" from "connected and showing the last frame forever" without a human looking at it.

Drive the canvas on a timer, not on requestAnimationFrame

This is the detail that costs an afternoon if you get it wrong. A background tab gets no animation frames, so a requestAnimationFrame draw loop stops the moment the tab is not visible — and the self-test then fails with a black or frozen viewer that has nothing to do with the network:

// Timer-driven, not requestAnimationFrame: a background tab gets no animation
// frames, which would silently stop the source and make the test look broken.
draw();
setInterval(draw, 33);

A 33 ms interval is roughly 30 fps and keeps producing frames while the tab is hidden, which is exactly when people leave a test running.

Count liveness two ways, because one of them stops in a hidden tab

requestVideoFrameCallback is the most accurate way to count painted frames, and it also stops firing when the tab is backgrounded. So count both painted frames and decoded frames, and let the test pass if either one is advancing:

if (video.requestVideoFrameCallback) {
  video.requestVideoFrameCallback(function tick() {
    painted += 1;            // frames the user could actually see
    video.requestVideoFrameCallback(tick);
  });
}

// getStats framesDecoded keeps advancing in a background tab.
setInterval(async () => {
  const s = await sample(pc, prev);
  prev = s;
  decoded = s.framesDecoded || 0;
}, 1000);

One counter answers "can the user see it", the other answers "is the decoder still receiving". Using only the first produces a test that fails whenever it is not being watched, which trains everyone to ignore it.

Give every run its own room

If the server enforces one publisher per room — and the simple SFU design does — then two concurrent self-tests collide: the second publisher evicts the first, and both tests report a failure that is really a scheduling coincidence.

Derive the room name per visit instead of hardcoding it:

const ROOM = 'selftest-' + (
  globalThis.crypto?.randomUUID?.() ||
  Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10)
);

That one line makes the test safe to run in parallel across browser tabs, machines and CI jobs with no coordination.

Mirror the state so automation can assert it

A test whose only output is pixels cannot be automated. Publish the state on a global object and assert on numbers:

const st = {
  publisher: 'connecting',
  viewer: 'connecting',
  frames: 0,      // frames painted, via requestVideoFrameCallback
  decoded: 0,     // frames decoded, via getStats - works in a background tab
  w: 0,
  h: 0,
  kbps: null,
  ice: '',
};
window.__st = st;

Now the assertion is boring and reliable: wait for ice to be connected, wait for decoded to exceed a threshold, and confirm the resolution is what you asked for. A driver script can do that in a few lines, and a failure tells you which of the three did not happen.

What this test does and does not prove

It proves the path end to end: track creation, offer/answer through the server, the SFU's fan-out, decoding, and the resolution and bitrate the session settled on. It catches the majority of regressions, because most of them break the path rather than a corner of it.

It does not prove TURN works from outside your network — that needs a host with a different NAT, which is why the relay probe is a separate test. It does not prove camera or microphone behaviour, because there is no camera. And it does not prove quality under loss; for that you need a network emulator, not a loopback.

Those boundaries are worth stating in the test itself. A self-test that claims to cover everything gets trusted for everything and then quietly lies.

The fixture, in order

  1. Source from a canvas, not a camera — headless, no permissions, no HTTPS requirement.
  2. Draw a moving element and a monotonic timestamp so a frozen frame cannot pass.
  3. Drive the canvas with a timer, because a hidden tab stops animation frames.
  4. Count painted frames and decoded frames, and accept either as liveness.
  5. Give each run a unique room so parallel tests cannot evict each other.
  6. Expose the state on a global so assertions are numeric, not visual.
  7. Be explicit about what the test does not cover, and keep the relay and loss tests separate.

This loopback test ships with the self-hosted WebRTC kit — canvas publisher, server relay, viewer, and the same stats panel the production viewer uses — so the whole path can be verified before a camera or a network is involved:

https://lowlatencykit.com/

The free relay probe, which covers the one thing the loopback test cannot, needs no account:

https://lowlatencykit.com/test/turn/

articles.title: Angular 🤝 Preact: The Ultimate Team
articles.description: Why Angular and Preact?   Building scalable and maintainable frontend applications becomes a...
articles.body_html:
Why Angular and Preact?

Building scalable and maintainable frontend applications becomes a difficult task when the framework is too opinionated or too loose. The goal is to provide familiar patterns on both sides while sacrificing nothing. Once thought to be nigh impossible is now brought into fruition by bridging similarities between two very different frameworks.

Angular thrives on structural architecture design and enforcing boundaries that make sense for large scale applications. We know through many years that MVC is a solid pattern not to be dismissed easily. We also know that through many years of exploring flexible developer experiences that React's ability to adapt is unrivaled. Where these two can come together is through Preact's Signals library and combining the efforts that Angular and React have honed into a solid set of practices.

Angular's architecture, rendered by Preact: modules, DI, and class views without the template compiler

Pick a side, the industry says. Want structure? Buy the whole framework:
template compiler, DI container, opinionated everything, and a migration
path when the ecosystem moves on without you. Want flexibility? Assemble
it yourself: but the structure you improvise at ten files becomes tribal
knowledge at a hundred, and the conventions that kept things tidy exist
only in the senior dev's head. Frameworks sell you structure or
freedom, and quietly charge you for the one you gave up.

PreactMVC refuses the trade. It gives you Angular's structural
machinery (hierarchical injectors, module ownership, an enforced MVC
split) as a library over ordinary Preact: opt into scope enforcement
where it pays, and stay plain JSX everywhere else. Signals replace
change detection, every Preact library works unmodified, and the same
view classes optionally render inside Web Workers as islands. The sales
pitch in one sentence: this is structure you call, not structure you
join.

Flexibility: render() is just Preact 

// counter.view.tsx
import { Component, Controller, View, inject, signal } from '@preact-mvc/core';

@Controller()
class CounterController {
  count = signal(0);
  inc = () => this.count.value++;
}

@Component({ controllers: [CounterController] })
export class CounterView extends View {
  private c = inject(CounterController);

  render() {
    return <button onClick={this.c.inc}>count: {this.c.count.value}</button>;
  }
}

A view is a class constructed once per mount inside its own injector
scope: inject() in field initializers, signals as plain fields, and a
render() that stays plain JSX forever. No hooks rules, no deps arrays,
no memoization audits. Construction is setup; render is projection.

And because render() returns ordinary Preact vnodes, flexibility
extends to the ecosystem itself. Icon sets, UI kits, preact/compat
React shims: drop them in. Function components keep their hooks and get
useService/useController/Provide as bridges into the injector.
Signal-aware libraries subscribe directly: our signals are
@preact/signals. Everything else takes two moves: provide the client
through DI, bridge subscribe into a scope-bound signal. The enterprise
demo runs TanStack Query, ECharts, zod, and a Tailwind/shadcn layer with
zero adapter packages: that is what "no lock-in" looks like measured.

Structure: the injector graph is the app map 

@Module({
  imports: [RouterModule.forRoot(routes), QueryModule.forRoot()],
  providers: [SessionService],              // scoped here, visible down
  controllers: [DashboardController],       // shared by this module's views
  components: [DashboardView],              // may only mount in this scope
  bootstrap: [DashboardView],
})
export class DashboardModule {}

components is an ownership declaration, not a registry: a declared
view refuses to mount outside an injector carrying its module. That is
the difference between structure as convention and structure as
contract: the architecture diagram is enforced at mount time, not
reviewed at PR time.

Providers are Angular's shapes: a class, { provide, useClass },
{ provide, useValue }, { provide, useFactory, deps }. Resolution
walks view scope, module scopes, root. DestroyRef ties teardown to the
scope, so a subscription created in a constructor dies with the view:
the same guarantee useEffect cleanup reaches for, made declarative.

The @Controller layer completes the MVC split Angular implied but
never enforced: controllers own interaction state, views project
signals, injectable stores own domain state. Declaration decides
lifetime: transient, view-scoped, or module-shared.

Structure that bends: opt out wherever it pays

The strictness is per-declaration, not global:

  • Undeclared views mount anywhere. components is opt-in enforcement, not a gate: skip it and the view is just a value you import, function components included.
  • Standalone views carry their module. @Component({ imports }) pulls a module's providers into one view's scope, so a feature can exist with no owning module at all.
  • The router is a module too. RouterModule.forRoot(routes) is a provider import, and routes can mount either a loose component or a full module with its own injector.

You buy structure exactly where you need it: the payment boundary, the
admin surface, the team's shared feature. Everything else stays the
JSX you would have written anyway.

Why use this?

Because the alternative is choosing between a framework that owns your
codebase and one that leaves it ungoverned. PreactMVC is for
developers who want the module map, the injector scoping, and the MVC
discipline: priced as four small packages, rendered by the 3kB engine
you already trust, compatible with the ecosystem you already use.

npm install -g @preact-mvc/cli
pmvc new my-app --islands
cd my-app && pmvc serve

The docs site walks DI, views, signals, the router, and the islands
contract end to end, with the demo and enterprise apps embedded live.

articles.title: The six getStats numbers that actually tell you what broke
articles.description: getStats() returns a few hundred fields across dozens of records, and almost all of them are useless...
articles.body_html:
getStats() returns a few hundred fields across dozens of records, and almost all of them are useless for diagnosis. The problem is not that the data is missing. It is that the numbers which matter only mean something in combination, and a dashboard that prints all of them tells you nothing.

These are the six worth putting on a screen, in the order I would look at them.

The whole thing in one line: the selected candidate pair tells you the path, the inbound counters tell you whether media arrived, and the outbound reason tells you why the encoder is holding back.

1. The selected candidate pair, and the candidate types behind it

This is the one everyone gets wrong, because getStats() reports many candidate-pair records and only one of them is the path your media is actually on. Print the wrong pair and you will confidently announce a direct connection while the session is relayed, or the reverse:

stats.forEach((r) => {
  if (r.type === 'local-candidate' || r.type === 'remote-candidate') cands[r.id] = r;
  if (r.type === 'candidate-pair' && (r.selected || r.state === 'succeeded') && r.currentRoundTripTime != null) {
    pair = r;
  }
});

Note the extra condition. Requiring currentRoundTripTime != null filters out pair records that exist but never carried a round trip — which is most of them on a NAT-heavy session. Without it, a "succeeded" pair with no measured RTT can win and you report a path that was never used.

The types are not on the pair. They live in separate records that the pair refers to by id, so you have to join them:

const l = cands[pair.localCandidateId];
const rm = cands[pair.remoteCandidateId];
out.localType = l ? l.candidateType : null;   // host | srflx | prflx | relay
out.remoteType = rm ? rm.candidateType : null;

host → host means a direct path on the same network. relay → relay means both sides are going through TURN, which is the expected state behind a carrier NAT and the first thing to verify when someone says the relay is broken. Skipping the join is why people conclude "it is always relayed" or "it is never relayed".

2. Inbound bitrate, which requires two samples

bytesReceived is a cumulative counter. You cannot read a rate out of a single snapshot, which is why so many quick debugging scripts print a number that keeps growing and call it bitrate:

// Pass the previous sample in; the delta is the rate.
if (prev && prev.bytes != null && r.bytesReceived != null && now > prev.t) {
  out.bitrateKbps = Math.round(((r.bytesReceived - prev.bytes) * 8) / (now - prev.t));
}
out.bytes = r.bytesReceived;

One unit trap lives in that line: (bytes delta * 8) / milliseconds is kilobits per second only because the division by a duration in milliseconds yields bits per millisecond — which is bits per second divided by a thousand. Get the units wrong here and your numbers are off by 1000, which looks like a codec problem.

3. framesPerSecond and resolution

These tell you whether the stream is alive at the quality you asked for. A stream that negotiated 1280×720 and settles at 320×180 is not broken; it is being told to back off, and the next two numbers say by what.

Read frameWidth/frameHeight from the inbound video record rather than from the video element's videoWidth. The element reports the decoded frame, which lags behind a change and is zero until the first frame decodes — the exact moment you most need a number.

4. qualityLimitationReason on the outbound side

This is the single most underused field in WebRTC diagnostics. When the encoder reduces resolution or frame rate, it says why:

if (r.type === 'outbound-rtp' && r.kind === 'video') {
  out.qlr = r.qualityLimitationReason || null;   // bandwidth | cpu | other | none
  ...
}

bandwidth means the estimator decided the path cannot carry more, and the fix is the network or the bitrate ceiling. cpu means the sender could not encode fast enough, and the fix is on the machine — resolution, hardware encoding, or too many tabs doing the same thing. other is usually a screen-share capture path that cannot keep up. Those are three different investigations, and without this field you are guessing between them.

5. framesDecoded versus framesReceived

This pair is how you separate transport from decode. Packets arriving while decoded frames stay flat means the media reached you and could not be turned into pictures — codec parameters, a missing keyframe, or a hardware decoder that gave up.

out.freezeCount = r.freezeCount != null ? r.freezeCount : null;
out.framesDecoded = r.framesDecoded != null ? r.framesDecoded : null;

freezeCount is the browser's own opinion that the picture stopped, which is a useful cross-check on your own frame-gap detection. If your 2-second frame-gap timer says "frozen" and freezeCount is still rising while framesDecoded is not, you are looking at decode, not at the network. If framesDecoded is climbing and the user still reports a frozen tile, the problem is downstream of the decoder — rendering, the element, or the application.

6. Jitter and the jitter buffer

Jitter on its own is a poor number to alarm on, because a jitter buffer exists precisely to absorb it. The informative value is the average time a frame spent waiting in that buffer, which you compute from two counters:

if (r.jitterBufferDelay != null && r.jitterBufferEmittedCount) {
  out.jbufMs = Math.round((r.jitterBufferDelay / r.jitterBufferEmittedCount) * 1000);
}

That is total buffer delay divided by frames emitted, scaled to milliseconds: the average per-frame hold. A buffer sitting in the tens of milliseconds is doing its job. A buffer climbing into the hundreds means the network is delivering frames unevenly enough that latency is the price being paid to keep the picture smooth — and for a live support call, that trade is often the wrong one.

The table that fits on one screen

The rendering that is actually useful is thirteen rows and no graphs:

const rows = [
  ['Connection',     (s.connState || '-') + ' / ' + (s.iceState || '-')],
  ['Bitrate in',     s.bitrateKbps != null ? s.bitrateKbps + ' kbps' : '-'],
  ['Resolution',     s.w ? s.w + ' x ' + s.h : '-'],
  ['FPS in',         s.fps != null ? s.fps + ' fps' : '-'],
  ['Packets lost',   s.loss != null ? s.loss : '-'],
  ['Jitter',         s.jitterMs != null ? s.jitterMs + ' ms' : '-'],
  ['Jitter buffer',  s.jbufMs != null ? s.jbufMs + ' ms' : '-'],
  ['RTT',            s.rttMs != null ? s.rttMs + ' ms' : '-'],
  ['Path',           s.localType ? s.localType + ' -> ' + s.remoteType : '-'],
  ['Freezes',        s.freezeCount != null ? s.freezeCount : '-'],
  ['Bitrate out',    s.outKbps != null ? s.outKbps + ' kbps' : '-'],
  ['FPS out',        s.outFps != null ? s.outFps + ' fps' : '-'],
  ['Quality limit',  s.qlr != null ? s.qlr : '-'],
];

Sampled once a second, that table answers the questions support actually asks: is there a path, is media arriving, at what quality, and if it is degraded, is the encoder blaming the network or the CPU.

How to read it in one pass

  1. Path shows the candidate types. relay -> relay on a cellular session is correct, not a bug.
  2. Bitrate in and FPS in flat or zero with Connection connected is a media problem, not a signaling problem.
  3. Frames received climbing while Frames decoded stays flat means the media arrived and could not be decoded.
  4. Quality limit: bandwidth and Quality limit: cpu are different bugs with different owners.
  5. A jitter buffer in the hundreds of milliseconds is the latency you are paying for smoothness.
  6. Freezes rising is the browser agreeing with your own freeze detection.

I built this sampling and rendering into the diagnostics panel of a self-hosted WebRTC kit, next to the recovery ladder that acts on it — ICE restart first, full rejoin when that fails — so the numbers are visible while the failure is happening rather than reconstructed from a log afterwards:

https://lowlatencykit.com/

The guide that covers the network layers these numbers are measuring is here:

https://lowlatencykit.com/guides/remote-field-assist-mobile-webrtc/

articles.title: The "Health Check" of a PCB: From AOI to X-Ray to Functional Test
articles.description: At AnyPCBA, every board goes through a "health check" before it leaves the factory.  This isn't a...
articles.body_html:
At AnyPCBA, every board goes through a "health check" before it leaves the factory.

This isn't a single step—it's a chain of inspections: AOI, X-Ray, ICT, and FCT. Each one answers the same question: is this board safe to ship?

But many engineers have a fuzzy understanding of this chain. They know the factory "tests it," but not exactly what's tested, what can be caught, and what can't.

This article breaks down the inspection chain, layer by layer: what each test does, what it can catch, and what it can't.

Layer 1: AOI—Visible Defects Don't Stand a Chance

AOI (Automated Optical Inspection) is the first layer of the chain.

The principle is simple: high-resolution cameras capture the PCB surface and compare it against a "golden reference" image to find differences. It inspects visible solder joints and components.

What AOI can catch:

  • Missing or misaligned components: a component that wasn't placed, or placed incorrectly
  • Solder bridges: two pins that shouldn't be connected, connected by solder
  • Insufficient solder or cold joints: weak or insufficient solder joints
  • Tombstoning: a component standing on one end
  • Polarity errors: diodes, capacitors, or ICs placed in the wrong orientation

AOI is fast and high-coverage, well-suited for high-volume inspection. But its limitation is obvious: it can only see the surface.

For BGA and QFN packages, where the solder joints are hidden beneath the package body, AOI is helpless. The joints are under the chip—the camera can't see them.

Layer 2: X-Ray—Seeing Through the Joints
X-Ray inspection exists to solve AOI's blind spot.

X-Ray uses the penetrating power of X-rays to "see through" BGA bottoms, QFN bottoms, and through-hole interiors. It inspects solder joint quality hidden beneath packages.

What X-Ray can catch:

  • BGA voiding: bubbles inside solder balls, affecting mechanical strength and thermal conductivity
  • Solder ball bridging: adjacent balls under a BGA connected together
  • Missing or shifted solder balls: balls that should be there but aren't, or are misaligned
  • Poor via filling: incomplete fill inside vias, affecting reliability
  • QFN bottom joint defects: poor soldering on the thermal pad under the chip

X-Ray's limitation: it can see the "shape" of a solder joint, but it's hard to directly judge "strength" and "electrical performance." A joint that looks normal may actually be a cold joint.

Layer 3: ICT—Checking Electrical Connections

ICT (In-Circuit Test) uses probes to contact test points on the board and measure electrical parameters point by point.

It checks circuit connection integrity and component electrical performance.

What ICT can catch:

  • Opens: connections that should exist but don't
  • Shorts: connections that shouldn't exist but do
  • Component value deviation: actual resistance or capacitance outside spec
  • Component orientation errors: polarized components placed backwards
  • Missing components: components that should be installed but aren't

ICT's core metric is "coverage." Ideally, every electrical net should have a test point. But in reality, high-density boards have limited test point space, and coverage often falls short of 100%. Insufficient test point coverage means some defects may slip through.

Layer 4: FCT—Verifying Function

FCT (Functional Circuit Test) is the last layer—and the closest to "real-world use."

It powers up the board, simulates actual operating conditions, and verifies whether the board functions correctly.

What FCT can catch:

  • Functional abnormalities: a functional module that doesn't work
  • Performance below spec: excessive output noise, insufficient response speed
  • Timing issues: power-up sequencing or signal timing that doesn't meet requirements
  • Boundary condition failures: abnormal operation under extreme temperature or voltage

FCT's key lies in test case design. The more comprehensive the test cases, the more potential problems are caught. If test cases only cover "normal operating conditions," boundary condition issues will be missed.

One Chain, Different Roles, None Optional

Looking at all four inspections together, their roles are clear:


No single inspection is universal. AOI can't see BGA bottoms. X-Ray can't see electrical performance. ICT can't see functional behavior. FCT can't see long-term reliability.

That's why the chain must be complete. Each inspection covers the blind spot of the one before it.

What This Means for Hardware Engineers

1. Test coverage determines recall rate. If you only do AOI, BGA-related defects will slip through. If you only do ICT, functional abnormalities will slip through.

2. Test point design must happen at the design stage. ICT coverage depends on test point accessibility. If test points aren't reachable, even the best ICT equipment is useless.

3. FCT test cases must cover boundary conditions. Testing only "normal operating conditions" isn't enough. Temperature boundaries, voltage boundaries, and timing boundaries are all potential failure points.

4. Understand the boundaries of each inspection. Don't expect any single inspection to "handle everything." The value of the chain lies precisely in each inspection knowing what it can't see.

At AnyPCBA, our inspection chain covers AOI, X-Ray, ICT, and FCT, serving small-to-medium volume PCB and PCBA projects from 5 to 5000 pieces.

Specifically, what we can support includes:

  • Full AOI inspection: every board goes through automated optical inspection before shipment, checking component placement, solder joint quality, and polarity
  • X-Ray inspection: for BGA, QFN, and other hidden-joint packages, providing void rate, bridging, and offset detection
  • ICT testing: based on the customer's test point design, providing in-circuit test fixtures and test programs
  • FCT functional testing: working with customers to define test cases covering normal operating conditions and boundary conditions
  • Test point accessibility review: checking test point layout during DFM review, catching coverage gaps early
  • Test fixture design and fabrication: for small-to-medium volume projects, providing fast, low-cost test fixture solutions

Our manufacturing capabilities cover 2–64 layers, including HDI, rigid-flex, and high-frequency hybrid. We hold ISO 13485 (medical) and IATF 16949 (automotive) certifications. If you're working on a PCB or PCBA project that needs a complete inspection chain, contact us through our website.

What defects have slipped through inspection in your projects? Share your experience in the comments.
